title: Lecture 17: Gambler’s ruin
text:
At the beginning of the class, it was likely mentioned that gambling is a bad idea. With your ample knowledge of probability theory, we can quantify how bad of an idea it is.






ImportantTheorem



Gambling with fair coin.
If two players start with a fixed number of dollars (\(n_A\) and \(n_B\) dollars respectively), and play a gambling game where one dollar is transferred from person A to B probability \(1/2\), and B to A otherwise. The game ends when one person ends up with everything. Then, the probability of person A winning the game is \[\frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}\] and the probability of person B winning is: \[\frac{n_B}{n_A + n_B}\]



Proof. Proof. (Hint: Call the (random) amount of money person A possesses after \(t\) rounds is \(X_t\). What is \(\mathbb{E}[X_{t+1}]\) in terms of \(\mathbb{E}[X_t]\)? ◻







ImportantTheorem



Gambling with unfair coin.
If two players start with a fixed number of dollars (\(i\) and \(N-i\) dollars respectively), and play a gambling game where one dollar is transferred from person A to B probability \(1/2\), and B to A otherwise. The game ends when one person ends up with everything. Then, the probability of person A winning the game is \[\frac{1-a^{i}}{1-a^{N}},\] where \(a=q/p\), the relative odds of person B winning.



Proof. Proof. (Hint: Call \(P_i\) the probability that person \(A\) will win if they start with \(i\) dollars. How does \(P_i\) relate to \(P_{i+1}\) and \(P_{i-1}\)?) ◻







TipExample



If a person walks into a casino with \(5\) dollars and plays the aforementioned game, how likely it is to double their fortune, when ..

The casino is 1.1 times likely to win a given game.
The casino is 2 times likely to win a given game.

title: Lecture 15: MGFs and probability inequalities
text:
For a random variable \(X\), the means (expectations) of powers \(X^k\) – called moments – have useful theoretical properties, and some of them are used for additional summaries of a distribution. The moment generating function is a related tool that aids in deriving distributions of sums of independent random variables and limiting properties of distributions.
First of all, we already know about \(k=1,2\), i.e. the first and second moments. The expectation of \(X\) is \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X^k]\) with \(k=1\). The variance of \(X\) is \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^k]\) with \(k=2\).






NoteDefinition



Moments.
\(\mathbb{E}[X^k]\) for \(k=1,2,...\)








NoteDefinition



Central moments.
\(\mathbb{E}[ (X - \mathbb{E}(X))^k]\) for \(k=2,3,...\)


Next, we see that if the \(k\)’th moment exists, all lower moments also exist.






ImportantTheorem



If \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^k] < \infty\) for some positive integer \(k\), then \[\mathbb{E}[|X|^j] < \infty\] for every positive integer \(j \le k\).


The conclusion also holds for non-integer \(j\) and \(k\). If \(\mathbb{E}[X^2] < \infty\), then both expectation and variance of \(X\) exist.

Proof. Proof. Hint: apply Jensen’s inequality. ◻

Is it possible to summarize all the information of moments with one function?
How to compute/summarize higher moments in a more general fashion?






NoteDefinition



Moment generating function (mgf) of \(X\): for real \(t\), \[\psi_X(t) = \mathbb{E}(e^{tX}) .\]


Immediately, \(\psi_X(0)=1\) for all random variable \(X\).
As the moment generating function is the expectation of a function of \(X\), it is possible that mgf does not exist for certain random variables.
It turns out the moment generating function is a defining feature of random variables, provided that it exists. The following theorem states that if the mgfs of two random variables are finite and identical for all values of \(t\) near \(t = 0\), then they must be distributed the same:






ImportantTheorem



If \(\psi_{X_1} (t)=\psi_{X_2}(t)\) for \(t\) in some neighborhood around \(t=0\), then \[X_1 \overset{d}{=} X_2.\] That is, \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) have the same distribution (up to a null set).








TipExample



Find the mgf for the following distributions:

Bernoulli
Exponential









ImportantTheorem



If \(\psi(t)<\infty\) for all values of \(t\) in some open interval around \(t=0\), then \[\mathbb{E}[X^k] < \infty,\] and, for \(k=1,2,...\), \[\mathbb{E}[X^k] = \psi^{(k)}(0).\]








TipExample



Find the first two moments for the following random variables with mgfs.

Bernoulli
Exponential



Next, here are some useful properties of moment generating functions:

A linear transformation of \(X\) has mgf: \[\psi_{aX+b}(t) = e^{bt}\psi_{X}(at)  .\]
The mgf of a sum of independent random variables is: \[\psi_{\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^nX_i}(t) = \prod\nolimits _{i=1}^n
    \psi_{X_i}(t)  .\]







TipExample



Suppose \(\{X_i, i=1,\cdots,n\}\) are independent; what is the mgf of \(\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n a_i X_i+b\)?








TipExample



Suppose \(X \sim Bin(n,p)\). What is the moment generating function \(\psi_X(t)\) of \(X\)?








TipExample



If \(X\) has the normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) and if \(Y= aX + b\) for constants \(a\neq 0\) and \(b\), prove that \(Y\) (1) has mean \(a\mu + b\) and variance \(a^2\sigma^2\), and (2) has the normal distribution.








TipExample



Suppose \(X_1\) is the number of heads from \(3\) coin flips with a biased coin (whose probability of heads is \(0.3\)). Also repeat the experiment with the same coin, but \(5\) times, and call \(X_2\) the resulting number of heads.

Prove directly that the sum \(X_1+X_2\) is distributed the same as if you flipped 8 time in the first place (i.e. \(\text{Binom}(8, 0.3)\)).
Prove this using mgfs.

title: Lecture 15: MGFs and probability inequalities
text:
Probability Inequalities [DS 6.2] [Lec 15]
Inequalities are useful for bounding probabilities that might otherwise be hard to compute. They will also be used in the theory of convergence in the next section.






ImportantTheorem



Markov.
Suppose \(X\) is a non-negative random variable (and \(a>0\)); then, \[\mathbb{P}(X \ge a) \le \mathbb{E} [X]/a.\]


Markov inequality is a fundamental inequality and can be used to show Chebyshev inequality.






ImportantTheorem



Chebyshev.
For random variable \(X\) whose variance exists, \[\mathbb{P}(|X-\mathbb{E}[X] |>t ) \le V(X)/t^2.\]



Proof. Proof. Apply Markov inequality. ◻







TipExample



\(2\sigma\) or \(3\sigma\) principle.
The \(2\sigma\) or \(3\sigma\) principle states that: no matter what the distribution is, a minimum of 75% of values must lie within two standard deviations of the mean, and 88.89% within three standard deviations.


Chernoff.
Hoeffding.






TipExample



Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n \sim Bernoulli(p)\). Let \(n = 100\) and \(\epsilon = .2\). Bound the probability that the average will be different from \(p\) by at least \(\epsilon\): \[P(|\bar X_n- p| > \epsilon) = ?.\]


Mill’s inequality.






ImportantTheorem



Schwartz inequality.
Suppose \(\mathbb{E}(XY) < \infty\), \[[\mathbb{E}(XY)]^2\le \mathbb{E}[X^2] \mathbb{E}[Y^2],\] where “\(=\)” is attained if and only if \(X=aY\) for some constant \(a\neq 0\) w.p. 1.


Plugging in \(X \leftarrow X-\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(Y \leftarrow Y-\mathbb{E}[Y]\), we get the following theorem.






ImportantTheorem



Cauchy-Schwartz inequality.
Suppose \(\sigma_X^2,\sigma_Y^2 < \infty\), \[[cov(X,Y)] ^2 \le  \sigma_X^2 \sigma_Y^2,\] where “\(=\)” is attained if and only if \(X=aY+b\) for some constants \(a\neq 0, b\), w.p. 1.


An important consequence of Cauchy-Schwartz inequality is that the correlation coefficient is bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\).






TipExample



If \(X\) is the price of gas, and \(Y\) is the number of gallons of gas that will be used by Bob this month. The average price of gas is \(4.00\), with a standard deviation of \(1\), and the number of gallon of gas Bob uses is on average \(20\) gallons with a standard devation of \(3\). Then, \(XY\) is how much Bob will spend on gas. What can you say about \(XY\) using Cauchy-Schwartz?


Convex combination.
Convex function.
Jensen’s inequality.

title: Lecture 13: Expectations and Variance
text:
Given a random element \(X\), how to give a one-number summary of it?
Recall the concept of an average of some numbers (or weighted averages, weighted by some relative importance). In probability theory, the average of a random variable is called expectation. Expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) captures the center of a random variable.






NoteDefinition



Expectation.
For discrete random variable \(X\), \[\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum \nolimits_{x \in supp(X)} x f(x),\] provided \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\).
For continuous random variable \(X\), \[\mathbb{E}[X] = \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^\infty  xf(x)dx,\] provided \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\).


The discrete version is essentially a weighted average of \(X\), and the weights are the probabilities.
The expectation a random variable is also called the “mean” of that random variable.






TipExample



Find the expectation (mean) of the following random variables.

The random variable \(X=c\) with probability 1.
Bernoulli random variable with parameter \(p\).
Uniform on \([a,b]\).
The random variable \(X\) with pdf symmetric about 0.



Note that expectation can be non-existent, as the integral or the summation may not exist.
Cauchy distribution.






TipExample



Suppose the pmf of the random variable \(X\) satisfies \[f(x) \propto \frac{1}{x^2}, \text{ for } x=1, 2,....\] Prove that the expectation of \(X\) does not exist.


When do we know when the expectation of random variable \(X\) exists? One way is to recognize that \(E[X]\) is bounded if \(X\) itself is bounded. To be more specific, if \(P(X\ge a) =1\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X] \ge a\); if \(P(X\le a) =1\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X] \le a\). So clearly, expectation exists for all absolutely bounded random variables.






NoteDefinition



Moments.
For a random variable \(X\), the means of powers \(X^k\) are called moments, which have useful theoretical properties, and some of them are used for additional summaries of a distribution.


(Later, we will learn about the moment generating function which a related tool that aids in deriving distributions of sums of independent random variables and limiting properties of distributions.)
Next, the expectation of a function of the random variable can be computed as follows:






ImportantTheorem



Expected value of function \(h(X)\) of \(X\).  Suppose discrete \(X\sim f\), function \(h:\R \to \R\), then \[\mathbb{E} [h(X)] = \sum_{x \in supp(X)} h(x)f(x) ,\] if the sum is finite.
Suppose continuous \(X\sim f\), function \(h:\R \to \R\), then \[\mathbb{E} [h(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty h(x)f(x) dx,\] if the integral is finite.


This theorem is sometimes called the Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS).

The relation between the probability of an event \(E\) and expectation is characterized as follows. \[\mathbb{P}(E)  = \mathbb{E}[ 1_E] ,\] where \(1_E\) denotes the indicator function of \(E\).

Folded Normal.






TipExample



The square root rule.
Suppose a randomly chosen student’s exm score \(X\) follows Unif\([0,100]\). The instructor applies a transformation to the scores to curve them, using: \[Y=h(X) = 10\times \sqrt{X}.\] For a few concrete examples are: \(h(0)=0\), \(h(100)=100\), \(h(36) =60\), \(h(64)=80, \cdots .\)

Find the pdf of \(Y\), and compare it with \(f_X\).
Compare the expected score: \(EY-EX>0\)?
Compare the proportion of Fails.









ImportantTheorem



Expectation of function of multiple RVs.
Suppose \(Y=h(X_1,X_2,...,X_n)\), and continuous \({\bf{X}} \sim f\), \[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E} [h({\bf{X}})] =
    \int_{-\infty}^\infty ... \int_{-\infty}^\infty
    h(\mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x}) d\mathbf{x},\] if the integral is finite.
Suppose \(Y=h(X_1,X_2,...,X_n)\), and discrete \({\bf{X}} \sim f\), \[\mathbb{E}[Y] =\mathbb{E} [h(\mathbf{X})] =
    \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in supp(\mathbf{X})} h(\mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x}) ,\] if the sum is finite.








TipExample



Suppose a point \((X,Y)\) follows the uniform distribution on the square \([0,1]^2\). We hope to find the expected area of the rectangle determined by \((X,Y)\). That is to find \(\mathbb{E}[XY]\) .








TipExample



Suppose \(X,Y\distras{iid} Exp(\lambda)\), whose pdf is \(f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) and let \[Z=
  \begin{cases}
    3X+1 & \text{ if } X\ge Y \\
    6Y & \text{if } X< Y.
  \end{cases}\] Find \(\mathbb{E}[Z]\).


Next, we describe two properties of expectations.






ImportantTheorem



Linearity.  Expectation of a linear function of \(X\): \[\mathbb{E}[aX+b] = a \mathbb{E}[X] +b.\] Expectation of a linear function of \(\mathbf{X}\): \[\mathbb{E}[ \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n a_i X_i+b] = \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n
    a_i \mathbb{E}[X_i] +b\]


Linearity is a fundamental property of expectation, and it is a consequence of the integral operation.






TipExample



Find the expectation of Binomial random variable \(X\) with parameters \((n,p)\).








TipExample



Suppose a librarian randomly stacks \(k\) different books on the shelf with the labels of their titles. What is the expected number of books under the correct labels?


Next, when we have independent random variables






ImportantTheorem



Let \(X_1,...X_n\) be independent random variables. Then \[\mathbb{E}[\prod\nolimits_{i=1}^n X_i ] = \prod\nolimits_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[ X_i ]\]


Pause and think about the two theorems. They are quite different. The mean of the product of random variables is only the product of means when they are independent. However, the sum of random variables has an expectation regardless of independence.






TipExample



Suppose \((X,Y) \distras{iid} N(0,1)\), The distribution of \(X/Y\) is a Cauchy distribution, whose probability density is \(f(z) = 1/(\pi (1+z^2))\) for \(-\infty < z < \infty\). Find \(\mathbb{E}[X/Y]\).


The product property will be useful when we study moment generating functions.






TipExample



Suppose \((X,Y) \distras{iid} N(0,1)\), find \(\mathbb{E}[e^{aX+bY}]\).


We end by discussing a salient feature of the expected value.






ImportantTheorem



The expectation or mean \(E[X]\) predicts \(X\) with the lowest mean squared error (MSE).


Specifically, if you had to pick one value to predict the (inherently) random variable \(X\), you should pick the mean, since it is the value that incurs the smallest error. text:
Given a random element \(X\), how to give a one-number summary of it?
Recall the concept of an average of some numbers (or weighted averages, weighted by some relative importance). In probability theory, the average of a random variable is called expectation. Expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) captures the center of a random variable.






NoteDefinition



Expectation.
For discrete random variable \(X\), \[\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum \nolimits_{x \in supp(X)} x f(x),\] provided \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\).
For continuous random variable \(X\), \[\mathbb{E}[X] = \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^\infty  xf(x)dx,\] provided \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\).


The discrete version is essentially a weighted average of \(X\), and the weights are the probabilities.
The expectation a random variable is also called the “mean” of that random variable.






TipExample



Find the expectation (mean) of the following random variables.

Bernoulli random variable with parameter \(p\).
Uniform on \([a,b]\).

Note that expectation can be non-existent, as the integral or the summation may not exist.
Cauchy distribution.






TipExample



Suppose the pmf of the random variable \(X\) satisfies \[f(x) \propto \frac{1}{x^2}, \text{ for } x=1, 2,....\] Prove that the expectation of \(X\) does not exist.


When do we know when the expectation of random variable \(X\) exists? One way is to recognize that \(E[X]\) is bounded if \(X\) itself is bounded. To be more specific, if \(P(X\ge a) =1\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X] \ge a\); if \(P(X\le a) =1\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X] \le a\). So clearly, expectation exists for all absolutely bounded random variables.






NoteDefinition



Moments.
For a random variable \(X\), the means of powers \(X^k\) are called moments, which have useful theoretical properties, and some of them are used for additional summaries of a distribution.


(Later, we will learn about the moment generating function which a related tool that aids in deriving distributions of sums of independent random variables and limiting properties of distributions.)
Next, the expectation of a function of the random variable can be computed as follows:






ImportantTheorem



Expected value of function \(h(X)\) of \(X\).  Suppose discrete \(X\sim f\), function \(h:\R \to \R\), then \[\mathbb{E} [h(X)] = \sum_{x \in supp(X)} h(x)f(x) ,\] if the sum is finite.
Suppose continuous \(X\sim f\), function \(h:\R \to \R\), then \[\mathbb{E} [h(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty h(x)f(x) dx,\] if the integral is finite.


This theorem is sometimes called the Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS).

The relation between the probability of an event \(E\) and expectation is characterized as follows. \[\mathbb{P}(E)  = \mathbb{E}[ 1_E] ,\] where \(1_E\) denotes the indicator function of \(E\).

text:
Variance [DS 4.3] [Lec 13]
In reality, the center of a distribution is not informative enough about the random quantity. We are interested in the how spread out the random variable is. Variance captures the variability or spread of a random variable.






NoteDefinition



Variance.
Variance is defined as \[V[X] = \mathbb{E} [(X - \mathbb{E}[X]) ^2].\]


Other notations: \(Var(X)\), \(\sigma^2(X)\) or \(\sigma^2\) when there is no confusion.






NoteDefinition



Standard deviation.
Standard deviation: \(\sqrt{V[X]}\)


Note, since variance is defined as the expectation of a special function of \(X\), it is possible for variance to not exist (i.e. be infinite).






TipExample



Variance.
Find the variance of the following random variables.

The random variable \(X=c\) with probability 1.
Bernoulli with parameter \(p\).
Uniform on \([a,b]\).









ImportantLemma



Alternative expression of variance.
\[V[X] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2.\]



Proof. Proof. (Hint: Use definition directly.) ◻







TipExample



Variance.
Find the variance of the following random variables using the alternative expression of variance.

The random variable \(X=c\) with probability 1.
Bernoulli with parameter \(p\).
Uniform on \([a,b]\).



Here are some elementary properties of the variance:

\(V[X] \ge 0\) for all \(X\).
\(V[X]\) exists for all bounded random variable \(X\).
\(V[X] =0\) if and only if \(\mathbb{P}(X=c) =1\) for some constant \(c\) (i.e., \(X\) is a constant).

As with expectation, linear transformations of \(X\) have an easier variance formula.






ImportantTheorem



Variance of a linear function of \(X\): \[V[aX+b] = a^2 V[X]\]
Variance of a linear function of \(\mathbf{X}\) where \(\{X_i\}\) are independent: \[V\left[ \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n a_i X_i+b\right] = \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n a^2_i V[X_i]\]



Important special cases of the above theorem under independence are as follows.

The variance of the sum of independent random variables. For all \(i=1,...,n\), choose \(a_i=1\) and \(b=0\) to get, \[V\left[ \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n  X_i\right] = \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n
      V[X_i]  .\]
The variance of the sample mean. For all \(i=1,...,n\), choose \(a_i=1/n\) and \(b=0\) to see that, \[V\left[ \frac{1}{n}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n  X_i\right]
      =\frac{1}{n^2} \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n
      V[X_i] .\]
The variance of the sample mean when \(X_1, \cdots, X_n\) are iid1. For all \(i=1,...,n\), choose \(a_i=1/n\) and \(V[X_i]=\sigma^2\), and \(b=0\), so that: \[V\left[ \frac{1}{n}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n  X_i\right]
      =\frac{\sigma^2}{n} .\]








TipExample



Find the variance of the \(\text{Binom}(n,p)\) distribution.








TipExample



Suppose \(Z_1,Z_2,...,Z_n\) is a sequence of independent random variables, and \(Z_k \sim N(0,k)\) for \(k=1,...,n\). Find the variance of the sample mean \(\bar Z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\).

title: Lecture 11: Transformations of random variables
text:
Suppose we know the distribution of a random variable \(X\), but are actually interested in the distribution of a function \(h(X)\) of that random variable. For example, if \(X\) is the rate at which customers are served in a queue, then \(1/X\) is the average waiting time. We will learn about determining the distribution of the transformed random variable \(h(X)\).
We will handle discrete and continuous random variables separately. Let’s start with an example.






TipExample



Let \(X\) have a uniform distribution on the integers \(\{1,2,\cdots,
  9\}\). Suppose we define \(Y = |X-5|\), which measures how far \(X\) is from the middle of the distribution, \(5\). What is the probability that \(Y=1\)?


Next, let’s define a general procedure for discrete random variable \(X\) with pmf \(f_X(\cdot)\). First introduce the new random variable \(Y= h(X)\). Then, the pmf of \(Y\) is:
\[f_Y(y) = \mathbb{P}(Y=y) = \mathbb{P}(h(X)=y) =  \sum\nolimits _{\{x:h(x)=y\}} f_X(x) .\]






TipExample



Continue with the previous example where \(X\) is uniform on the integers \(\{1,2,\cdots, 9\}\) and \(Y = |X-5|\) What is the probability distribution of \(Y\)?


Next, for continuous random variable \(X\) with pdf \(f_X(x)\), let \(Y=h(X)\). Then, the cdf of \(Y\) is: \[F_Y(y) = \mathbb{P}(h(X) \le y) = \int_{\{x:h(x)\le y\}} f_X(x)dx .\] Also, we know now that pdf \(f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy}F_Y(y)\) for all \(y\) such that \(F_Y\) is differentiable.






ImportantTheorem



transformations of a univariate random variable.
“First principle” method for transforming a univariate random variable:

Suppose the transformed random variable \(Y=r(X)\) and we know \(f_X\). We find the cdf of \(Y\) by the definition of cdf: \[F_Y(y) = \mathbb{P}(Y\le y) = \mathbb{P}(r(X) \le y)
      = \int_{\{x:r(x)\le y\}} f_X(x) dx.\] This step applies for both discrete and continuous \(X\)’s.
If \(F_Y(y)\) is differentiable, we obtain pdf \(f_Y(y)\) by taking derivative: \(f_Y(y) = F^\prime_Y(y)\).
If \(F_Y(y)\) is not differentiable, we obtain pmf \(f_Y(y)\) by calculating the jumps of \(F_Y(y)\). Alternatively for discrete random variables, we could directly compute pmf \(f_Y(y)\) by the following steps: \[f_Y(y) = \mathbb{P}(Y=y) = \mathbb{P}(r(X) = y) = \mathbb{P}(X \in r^{-1}(y)).\]









TipExample



Find the distribution of \(Y\) in the following cases.

\(Y=X^2\) where \(X\sim \text{Unif}(-1,1)\).
Suppose \(X\sim N(0,1)\), find the distribution of \(Y_1 = e^X\), and \(Y_2 = X^2\).
Suppose \(X\sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\), find the distribution of \(Y = X^2\).



Folded Normal.
Next, when the transformation \(Y = r(X)\) is done by a special monotone function \(r\) that also has a derivative, there is a straightforward way to derive the distribution of \(Y = r(x)\).






ImportantLemma



monotonic and differentiable transformations.
 Suppose \(Y=r(X)\), and the transformation \(r(\cdot)\) is strictly monotonic and has an inverse \(s=r^{-1}\), then \[f_Y(y) = f_X(s(y)) |\frac{d}{dy} s(y)|.\]








TipExample

\(Y=aX+b\) if \(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x)\)?
\(Y=e^X\) if \(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x)\)?
\(Y=\log(X)\) where \(X\) is a strictly positive random variable with pdf \(f_X(x)\)?

title: Lecture 9: Bivariate distributions
text:
So far, we have mainly dealt with one random variable at a time. Let’s expand our toolset to deal with two or more variables at a time. First, let’s define a bivariate random vector of \(X\) and \(Y\).






NoteDefinition



Bivariate random vector.
\((X,Y): \Omega_{(X,Y)} \to \bR^2\).


Just like in one variable’s distribution (which has a cdf and pmf or pdf associated with it), a bivariate random vector \((X,Y)\) also has a distribution that describes its joint random behavior.






NoteDefinition



Joint distribution.
The joint distribution is defined as the collection of all probabilities of the form \(\mathbb{P}((X,Y) \in E)\) for all \(E \subset \bR^2\) such that \(\{(X,Y)
  \in E\}\) is an event.


We will start with the case where \(X\) and \(Y\) are both discrete, noting that all of the following are possible:

\(X\) and \(Y\) are both discrete.
\(X\) and \(Y\) are both continuous.
\(X\) is discrete, and \(Y\) is continuous.







NoteDefinition



Discrete joint distribution.

title: Lecture 7: Continuous RVs
text:
We have so far learned about discrete random variables.
But many random variables can take values in certain intervals. For instance, human height/weight measurements, temperature, precipitation, etc. We model these using continuous random variables.






NoteDefinition



continuous random variable.
The random variable \(X\) is continuous, if \(\exists\) a function \(f:
    \bR \to \R_+\) such that \[P(a \le X\le b) = \int_{a}^bf(x)dx .\] Probability density function (pdf): the above \(f\).


How is a pdf related to events’ probabilities? For continuous random variable \(X\), the probability of event \(E\) is \[\mathbb{P}(E) = \int \nolimits_{x\in E} f(x) dx.\]
It should be noted that a probability density function (pdf) is not the same as probability. For example, for a continuous random variable \(X\), \(P(X=a) =0\) but its pdf at \(a\) can be strictly positive.






NoteDefinition



Support.
Support of continuous random variable \(X\) is defined as the (closure of) \(\{x: f(x) >0\}\) where \(f(x)\) is the pdf.


It is also useful to note:

\(f(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \bR\), and
\(\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)dx =1\).

(Note, it naturally follows that \(\int_{supp(X)} f(x)dx =1\), since for values of \(x\) outside of the support, \(f(x)=0\).)
Sometimes we only know or recognize the pdf up to a constant (that is, constant with respect to \(x\)): \[f(x) =c(\theta) g_\theta(x),\] where \(g_\theta(x)\) is known, \(\theta\) is some constant (“parameter”). We can write this as \(f(x) \propto g_\theta(x)\).






NoteDefinition



Normalizing constant.
For pdf such that \[f(x) =c(\theta) g_\theta(x),\] \(c(\theta)\) is the normalizing constant.


Without the normalizing constant \(c(\theta)\), the pdf is incomplete. How to compute \(c(\theta)\) then? The idea is to use the property that: \[\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)dx =1.\]
(The same idea applies to pmfs, whose probabilities \(\sum_{x \in \text{Supp}(X)} f(x)dx =1\)






TipExample



For continuous random variable \(X\), \(f(x) \propto e^{-2x}\) for \(x>0\); \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\le 0\).

Compute the normalizing constant.
Compute \(P(1<X<2)\).



In order to fully specify a probability distribution, you must calculate the normalizing constant using the above technique. But often, the \(g_\theta(x)\) (sometimes called a “kernel”) is enough to identify a distribution. In fact, when you see that the kernel of one pdf matches that of another distribution, the two random variables are distributed the same.






TipExample



Identifying a distribution using kernel.
If the random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f_X(x) = c(n, p) \cdot p^x (1-p)^{n-x}\), what is the distribution of \(X\)?


Just as with discrete random variables, we can define the expectation of a continuous random variable as a probability-weighted average of the possible values.






NoteDefinition



Expectation.
For continuous random variable \(X\), \[\mathbb{E}[X] = \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^\infty  xf(x)dx,\] provided \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\).


We will put this to use soon.



In this section, we will introduce a few important distributions. Here is an extensive list of commonly used continuous random variables.

The Uniform distribution
Normal (Gaussian) distribution
Gamma distribution: special case is exponential (and chi-square.)
The \(\chi^2\) (Chi-squared) distribution
The Beta distribution: special case is uniform.
The student\(-t\) distribution (advanced)
Cauchy distribution (advanced)

We will introduce a few of these. Make sure to study the rest in DS section 3.2 and section 5. You will be tested on them.






NoteDefinition



Uniform.
The random variable \(X\) is uniform on \([a,b]\). Its pdf is \[f(x) = \frac{1}{b-a} 1_{x \in [a,b]}.\] We write \(X \sim U(a,b)\) or \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(a,b)\) or \(X \sim \text{Unif}(a,b)\).








TipExample



Expectation of uniform.
1. If random variable \(X\) is distributed as \(U(0,1)\), what is the expected value?
2. If you pick a random uniform value between \(a\) and \(b\), what is the expected value?


Next, the Normal distribution is one of the most relevant distributions for statistical modeling in a wide array of applictions.






NoteDefinition



Normal.
The random variable \(X\) has a Normal distribution with parameters \(\mu \in \mathbb R\) and \(\sigma \in \mathbb R^+\) if its pdf is \[f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2}}.\] We write \(X\sim \mathcal{N} (\mu, \sigma^2)\). Also, the Standard Normal distribution is the Normal distribution but with specific parameters \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma^2=1\).
(The two parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are sometimes called the mean and variance of the distribution.)








TipExample



Normal mean and variance.
We can see, from examining the pdf, that
1. A Normal random variable is symmetric around its mean \(\mu\),
2. The standard deviation parameter \(\sigma\) (square root of the variance) dictates the spread of the random variable’s potential values. (Use \(\mu = 0\) for simplicity.)


These distributions are the first ones we learn about whose pdf cannot be integrated in closed form. So, we need tables of the cdf values or computer programs in order to compute probabilities and quantiles for normal distributions.
Here are some basic properties of a Normal distribution.

A normal pdf is bell-shaped and symmetric around \(\mu\).
If \(X\) has the normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) and if \(Y= aX + b\) for constants \(a\neq 0\) and \(b\), then \(Y\) has the normal distribution with mean \(a\mu + b\) and variance \(a^2\sigma^2\). 1




Pdf of a Normal distribution.


Why is the Normal distribution so important? There are three reasons.
The first reason is directly related to the mathematical properties of the normal distributions. If a random samples (that is, many independent repeated random variables) are from a normal distribution, then the distributions of various important functions of the observations in the sample can be derived explicitly and have simple forms. title: Lecture 5: Random variables
text:
Let’s start with an example. Suppose that you flip a fair coin three times. The sample space for this experiment is
\[\Omega=\{H H H, H H T, H T H, H T T, T H H, T H T, T T H, T T T\} .\]
Since the coin is fair, we have that
\[P(\{H H H\})=P(\{H H T\})=\cdots=P(\{T T T\})=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}=\uline{\hspace{3em}}.%\frac{1}{8} .\]
Suppose that we are interested in a particular quantity associated to the experiment, say the number of tails that we observe. This is of course a random quantity. In particular, we can conveniently define a function \(X: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) that counts the number of tails. Precisely,
\[\begin{aligned}
& X(H H H)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& X(H H T)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& X(H T H)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& X(H T T)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& \vdots \\
& X(T T T)=\uline{\hspace{3em}}
\end{aligned}\]
Since the outcome of the experiment is random, the value that the function \(X\) takes is also random. That’s why we call a function like \(X\) a random variable1. \(P\) induces through \(X\) a probability distribution on \(\mathbb{R}\). In particular, we can easily see that the probability distribution of the random variable \(X\) is
\[\begin{aligned}
& P(X=0)=P(\{H H H\})=1 / 8 \\
& P(X=1)=P(\{H H T, H T H, T H H\})=3 / 8 \\
& P(X=2)=P(\{H T T, T H T, T T H\})=3 / 8 \\
& P(X=3)=P(\{T T T\})=1 / 8 \\
& P(X=\text { any other number })=0 .
\end{aligned}\]

title: Lecture 5: Random variables
text:
Introduction [DS 3.1] [Lec 5]
We have defined probability (measure) for events. In the framework of set theory, operations on sets are limited and we are in need of a more flexible modeling strategy. In contrast to the set theory, the mathematical theory of functions is mature and provides a convenient way for characterizing uncertainty and randomness.






NoteDefinition



Random variable.
A random variable (r.v.) is defined as a real function from sample space \(\Omega\) to real numbers \(\bR\). Suppose the random variable \(X\) is associated with the sample space \(\Omega\), \[X(\omega): \Omega \to \bR.\]


For any (measurable) event \(A\), \(X(A) = \{X(\omega): \omega\in A\} \subset \bR\).
For any subset \(B\) of \(\bR\), \(X^{-1}(B) =\{\omega \in \Omega: X(\omega) \in B\}\) is an event.




image









TipExample



Define random variables to represent the outcomes of the experiment.

Toss a coin, \(\Omega=\{H,T\}\), count the number of heads \(X(H) =1\), \(X(T)=0\).
Toss a coin multiple times, count the number of heads \(\Omega=\{HHH,TTT\}\), \(X(HHH) =3\), \(X(THT)=1\).
Roll a die; take the number of 3’s.
Human height measurement



Distribution.
When a probability measure has been specified on the sample space of an experiment, we can determine probabilities associated with the possible values of each random variable \(X\).
Let \(A\) be a subset of the real line such that \(\{X \in A\}\) is an event, and let \(\mathbb{P}(X \in A)\) denote the probability that the value of \(X\) will belong to the subset \(A\). Then \(\mathbb{P}(X \in A)\) is equal to the probability that the outcome \(s\) of the experiment will be such that \(X(s) \in A\). In symbols, \[\mathbb{P}(X \in A) = \mathbb{P}(\{s: X(s) \in A\})\]
The distribution of \(X\) is the collection of all probabilities of the form \(\mathbb{P}(X \in A)\) for all sets \(A\) of real numbers such that \(\{X \in A \}\) is an event.
Now equipped with the notion of a distribution, we can consider events in terms of values of the random variables, e.g. \(E = \{X: X \ge 3\}\).
The theory of random variable is developed in two parts. The first part is devoted to the discrete random variables, the second part is devoted to the continuous random variables.

title: Lecture 5: Random variables
text:
Discrete random variables [DS 3.1] [Lec 5]

Definition and Properties






NoteDefinition



discrete distribution.
We say that a random variable \(X\) has a discrete distribution, or that \(X\) is a discrete random variable if \(X\) can take only a finite number of different values.


(We also sometimes say that \(X\) is distributed as a discrete random variable of a particular name. More on this later.) Using discrete random variables, let’s describe the entire process:

An experiment has random outcomes. (Sample space \(\Omega\)). Events are collections of outcomes.

e.g. Flip coin 3 times. Getting all heads {HHH}, or getting exactly one tails {THH, HTH, HHT} are events.

Random variables encode the values associated with outcomes (maps it to the real line).

e.g. RV \(X\) that counts the number of heads in an experiment of three coin flips. \(X\) is a discrete random variable.

Probability \(\mathbb{P}(X \in A)\) measures the chances of a random variable \(X\) being in set \(A\). It is equivalent to \(\mathbb{P}(\{w: X(w) \in A\}\))

e.g. \(A = \{ x: x \ge 1\}\) for RV \(X\), and implicitly measures the chances of the event that 1 or more heads are obtained in the original coin flip experiment.








NoteDefinition



For discrete random variable \(X\), the probability function (pf) is \[f(x) = \mathbb{P}(X=x)\] for all \(x\in \bR\). The pf is also called probability mass function (pmf).


How is a pmf related to events’ probability? To compute the probability of event \(X \in E\), we simply add the probabilities of all the elements. \[\mathbb{P}(X \in E) = \sum \nolimits_{x\in E} f(x).\]






NoteDefinition



Support. Support of \(X\) is defined as (the closure of) the set \(\{x: f(x)>0\}\). Notation: \(supp(X)\).


Informally, the support is the values of \(X\) for which there is nonzero probability.






TipExample



It is useful to sketch a probability mass function (pmf). For the number of heads in two coin flips:


It is also useful to note:

if \(x\) is not one of the possible values of \(X\), then \(f(x) = 0\). (Thus, we only need to consider the support of the random variable, instead of the entire set of real numbers \(\bR\).)
\(\sum\nolimits_{x\in \text{supp}(X)}f(x) = 1\).
\(f(x) \in [0,1], \forall x \in \mathbb R\).

Lastly, looking ahead a bit, we’ll be learning about continuous random variables (say \(X\)) that can take values in an uncountably infinite set (i.e., not discrete) of values. We can calculate the probability that a continuous \(X\) is in an interval \((a,b]\) (for \(a<b\)) as: \[\mathbb{P}(X \in (a,b]) = \int_a^b f(x) dx,\] for a continuous probability function (called a probability density function, or pdf).
(Also notice that this implies that, for any single value \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(P(X=x) = 0\)! Weird, but we’ll get used to this.)






TipExample



What is \(\mathbb{P}(X \in (a,b])\) if \(X\) is a discrete random variable? For example, if you flip two coins, and \(X\) is the number of heads, what is \(\mathbb{P}(X
\in (0.5, 1])\)? What about \(\mathbb{P}(X \in (0,2])\)?


Note, it is possible for two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) to have nothing to do with each other, while having the same distribution (i.e., same probability mass function).
Suppose \(X\) is the random variable denoting the number of heads in a single dice roll. Also suppose \(Y\) is the number of heads from a subsequent roll. the distribution of \(X\) will be the same as the distribution of \(Y\), but \(Y\) is not like \(X\) in any other way. (They are clearly from completely different random experiments.)






TipExample



What is the probability mass function of \(X\) (and equivalently, of \(Y\))?




Important Discrete Random Variables (pt 1) [DS 3.1, DS 5] [Lec 5]
Discrete uniform distribution.
Next, we will learn some ‘named’ discrete distributions that are frequently used for probability modeling.
The symbol \(\sim\) is an identifier for a random variable, and specifies its pmf. In statistical jargon, we will say that a random variable has a certain distribution to signify that it has a a certain pmf (or pdf).






NoteDefinition



Bernoulli distribution.
Suppose you have a coin that, when flipped once, has a probability \(p \in [0,1]\) of yielding a head. Let’s call the event ‘seeing heads’ a success. The random variable \(X\) counts the number of heads: \[X =
   \begin{cases}
     1 & \text{ if heads } \\
     0 & \text{ if tails }.
   \end{cases}\] We write \(X\sim Bernoulli(p)\) or \(X\sim Bern(p)\).


The pmf of a Bernoulli random variable is \[f(x) =
\begin{cases}
   p^x(1-p)^{1-x} & \text{ if } x \in\{0,1\}\\
   0 &\text{ if } x \not \in \{0,1\}.
\end{cases}\]
We can also write the pmf succintly as \(P(X=x) = f(x) =
p^x(1-p)^{1-x}\). Q: Can you see why?






NoteDefinition



Binomial distribution.
Toss the same coin \(n\) times; in each trial, call the outcome a RV \(X_i \sim
   Bern(p)\). Then, the number of heads \(X\) we observe from \(n\) coin flips is \[X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i.\] We write \(X\sim Binom(n,\theta)\) or \(X\sim Bin(n,\theta)\).


The pmf of a binomial random variable is \[f(x) =
\begin{cases}
   {n \choose x} p^x(1-p)^{1-x} & \text{ if } x \in\{0,1,\cdots, n\}\\
   0 &\text{ if } x \not \in \{0,1,\cdots, n\}
\end{cases}\] Q: Can you see why the binomial coefficient is used?






TipExample



Prove that \(\sum_{x=0}^n f_X(x)=1\) for any binomial random variable.
(Hint: use the binomial theorem.)




Expectation [DS 4.1, DS 4.2] [Lec 5]






TipExample



An investor is considering buyingwhether or not to invest \(\$18\) per share in a stock for one year. The value of of this stock after one year will be \(18+X\), where \(X\) is the amount by which the price changes over the year. At present \(X\) is unknown (or random) and the investor would like to compute an “average value” for \(X\) in order to compare the return she expects from the investment to what she would get by putting the \(\$18\) in a bank at 5% interest.
What will be her average return at the bank? Is it random or deterministic?


The idea of finding an average value as in this example arises in many applications that involve a random variable. One popular choice is what we call the mean or expected value or expectation.
The intuition behind a mean of a random variable is that it is the weighted average of the possible values of the random variable with the weights equal to the probabilities.






TipExample



Suppose that the change in price of the stock in the previous example is a random variable \(X\) that can assume only the four different values \(-2,0,1\), and \(4\), and that \(\mathbb{P}(X=-2)=0.1, \mathbb{P}(X=0)=0.4,
    \mathbb{P}(X=1)=0.3\), and \(\mathbb{P}(X=4)=0.2\).
Then, what is the probability-weighted average of \(X\)? How does this compare to the expected return at the bank?


The calculation in this example generalizes easily to every random variable that assumes only finitely many values.






NoteDefinition



Expectation.
For discrete random variable \(X\), \[\mathbb{E}[X] =\sum \nolimits_{\text{All } x} x f(x) =  \sum \nolimits_{x \in supp(X)} x f(x),\] provided \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\).








TipExample



Find the expectation (mean) of the following random variables.

The random variable \(X=c\) with probability 1.
Bernoulli random variable with parameter \(p\).
Binomial random variable with parameter \(n\) and \(p\).



Note: We will revisit expectation in greater detail in a later lecture. In the meantime, you should read [DS 4.1-4.2] in advance.

title: Lecture 3: Counting methods
text:
It’s not always the case that outcomes of an experiment are equally likely.
However, when they are, we find it very useful to learn how to count the number of outcomes in the event, or in the sample space. Many classical probability calculations can be done by these methods.
Basic techniques from combinatorial analysis come in handy for this type of question. Let’s take a closer look to some relevant cases.
Suppose you have a group of \(m\) elements \(a_1, \cdots ,a_m\) and another group of \(n\) elements \(b_1, \cdots, b_n\). You can form \(mn\) pairs containing one element from each group. (Of course you can easily extend this reasoning to more than just two groups.) This is a useful fact when we are sampling with replacement and the order matters. Let’s make this formal.






ImportantTheorem



The multiplication rule.
Experiment with multiple stages, \(k\) stages; in stage \(i\), there are \(n_i\) options. In total, the number of options is \[\prod \nolimits_{i=1}^k n_i.\]








TipExample



What is the total number of outcomes?

rolling two dice
toss one coin and roll one die;
10-digit phone numbers





The total number of relevant outcomes may heavily depend on whether, in each of your \(k\) stages of your experiment, the items that have already been chosen so far can still be chosen.






NoteDefinition



Sampling with replacement.
Selecting/obtaining \(k\) items from a total of \(n\) items with replacement.


Let’s start with the simpler case of \(k=1\), i.e., selecting one item out of \(n\).
Suppose you toss a six-sided die twice. You have \(6\) simple outcomes on the first roll and \(6\) possible outcomes in the second roll.
In this type of problem, there are a few things to check.
1. Is the experiment performed with replacement? Yes; if the first roll is a \(2\), nothing precludes the fact that the second roll is a \(2\) again.
2. Does the order matter? Yes; the pair \((2,5)\) corresponding to a \(2\) on the first roll and a \(5\) on the second roll is not equal to the pair \((5,2)\) corresponding to a \(5\) on the first roll and a \(2\) on the second roll. We will revisit this when we learn about permutations.






TipExample



Suppose a box contains \(6\) numbered balls; for each selection, record the number and put the selected ball back to the box. Is this sampling with or without replacement? What is the total number of possible outcomes?


(Note, the experiment where you roll two fair dice is the same experiment as one dice being independently rolled twice.)
Next, what if the sampling is done without replacement?






NoteDefinition



Sampling without replacement.
Selecting \(k\) items from a total of \(n\) items without replacement.


Here is an example. We’d like to count how many different subsets of three people can become officers of an organization of \(n=30\) people, if chosen randomly? Order doesn’t matter here (we are not interested in the exact appointments for a given candidate). The random sampling of random three officers from \(n\) people is a sampling conducted without replacement.
Here are some other examples:

Texas Holdem: 3 common cards are dealt sequentially from a deck of cards. 2 cards are dealt to each player from the same deck.
Blackjack: 2 cards are dealt to each player from the same pile of cards.
Lotto numbers are drawn sequentially.




We will learn three tools for counting. This is called combinatorics, and is an elegant branch of mathematics that we borrow from.

Permutations
Combinations
Partitions

First, we use a core counting operation called factorials.






NoteDefinition



Factorial.
Factorial \(n!\) is defined as \[n! =n\times (n-1) \times ... \times 2 \times 1.\]


A factorial is useful for counting permutations.






NoteDefinition



All permutations.
The number of distinct orderings of \(n\) elements is \(n!\).


Next, we define permutation number \(P_{n,k}\), the way to order \(k\) elements chosen from \(n\) elements; also called \(k\)-permutation.






NoteDefinition



Permutation number.
Permutation number \(P_{n,k}\) is the number of distinct orderings such that \(k\) elements are selected from \(n\) items in order, without replacement. \[P_{n,k} =   n!/(n-k)! = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2), \cdots, (n-r+1).\] Note: Order matters!


Consider the example from before. There are 30 members in a student organization and they need to choose a president, a vice-president, and a treasurer. In how many ways can this be done? The size of the \(n\) distinct elements (persons) is \(n =
30\), the number of persons to be appointed is \(r = 3\). The sampling is done without replacement (a president is chosen out of \(30\) people, then among the \(29\) people left a vice-president is chosen, and finally among the \(28\) people left a treasurer is chosen).
Does the order matter? Yes, the president is elected first, then the vice-president, and finally the treasurer (think about ‘ranking’ the 30 candidates). The number of ways in which the three positions can be assigned is therefore \(P_{30,3} = 30!/(30-3)! = 30 \cdot 29 \cdot 28 = 24360.\)
Note, the number of ways to choose \(n\) out of \(n\) elements is \(P_{n,n}\) simplifies to \(n\) factorial (\(n!\)). In this case, no choosing occurs; we only need to count the ways to order.






TipExample



Choosing officers.
Suppose a club has 25 members, a president and a secretary are to be chosen from the membership. How many distinct configurations can we have?








TipExample



Bookshelf.
Suppose you have 10 books on your bookshelf, how many ways are there to arrange all of the books?








TipExample



Birthday problem.
What is the probability that at least two of the students in STAT131 have the same birthday?
Hint: \(E=\{\)at least two of the students have the same birthday\(\}\) and we are interested in \(\mathbb{P}(E)\).


Approximate factorials Most computers cannot handle \(n!\) and arithmetic operations when \(n\) is big. The trick is to complete the arithmetic operations in log-scale and exponentiate the results in the end.
To compute \(\frac{P_{n,k}}{n^k}\), we compute \(\log(P_{n,k}) - k \log (n)\) where \(\log(P_{n,k}) = \log(n!)-\log((n-k)!) = \sum_{i=n-k+1}^n\log(i)\). Identity: \(\frac{P_{n,k}}{n^k} = e^{\log(P_{n,k}) - k \log (n) }\) where \(\log(\cdot)\) is the natural log.






NoteDefinition



Combination number.
Suppose a set has \(n\) elements, select \(k\) elements without replacement. Each subset of size \(k\) is a combination of \(n\) elements taken \(k\) at a time. The number of distinct combinations: \[C_{n,k} = \frac{P_{n,k}}{k!} = \frac{n!} {(n-k)!k!}.\] Also known as binomial coefficients \(\binom{n}{k}\). Note: Order doesn’t matter!


The combination number is used in the famed binomial theorem.






ImportantTheorem



Binomial theorem.
\[(x+y)^n = \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{k} x^ky^{n-k}.\]








TipExample



Complete square: \((x+y)^2= ?\) and \((x+y)^3= ?\).








ImportantLemma



A few frequently used properties of binomial coefficients:

\(\binom{n}{0} = \binom{n}{n} =1\),
\(\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}\).
\(\binom{n}{k} + \binom{n}{k-1} = \binom{n+1}{k}\).
Vandermonde’s identity: \[\binom{m+n}{k} = \sum_{j=0}^k\binom{m}{j} \binom{n}{k-j}.\]









TipExample



Texas Holdem.
A 5-card hand is dealt from a standard, well-shuffled 52-card deck. The hand is called a full house in poker if it consists of three cards of some rank and two cards of another rank. e.g. three \(K\)’s + two 7’s, where ordering does not matter. What is the probability of a full house?








TipExample



Blood Alleles.
The gene for human blood type consists of a pair of alleles chosen from the three alleles commonly called O, A, and B. For example, two possible combinations of alleles (called genotypes) to form a blood-type gene would be BB and AO. We will not distinguish the same two alleles in different orders, so OA represents the same genotype as AO. How many genotypes are there for blood type?








TipExample



Fair coin tossed.
A fair coin is to be tossed 10 times. Determine the probability that exactly 3 heads will occur? Also determine the probability that three or fewer heads will occur?








TipExample



Sampling without replacement.
Suppose an urn contains 15 yellow and 30 blue balls, from which 10 balls will be selected at random. What is the probability that exactly three yellow balls will be selected?


Next, suppose we want to partition a set of \(n\) elements into \(r\) subsets so that the \(i\)’th subset contains \(n_i\) elements, and \(\sum_i n_i = n\). How many ways to do this?






NoteDefinition



Partitions.
The number of ways to partition \(n\) elements into \(n_1, \cdots, n_r\) groups is \[\binom{n}{n_1,\cdots, n_r}.\] This is the multinomial coefficient.


Q: Can you see how the combinations \(C_{n,k}\) are a specific case of partitions, so that the binomial coefficient is a specific case of the multinomial coefficient?

title: Lecture 3: Counting methods
text:
It’s not always the case that outcomes of an experiment are equally likely.
However, when they are, we find it very useful to learn how to count the number of outcomes in the event, or in the sample space. Many classical probability calculations can be done by these methods.
Basic techniques from combinatorial analysis come in handy for this type of question. Let’s take a closer look to some relevant cases.
Suppose you have a group of \(m\) elements \(a_1, \cdots ,a_m\) and another group of \(n\) elements \(b_1, \cdots, b_n\). You can form \(mn\) pairs containing one element from each group. (Of course you can easily extend this reasoning to more than just two groups.) This is a useful fact when we are sampling with replacement and the order matters. Let’s make this formal.






ImportantTheorem



The multiplication rule.
Experiment with multiple stages, \(k\) stages; in stage \(i\), there are \(n_i\) options. In total, the number of options is \[\prod \nolimits_{i=1}^k n_i.\]








TipExample



What is the total number of outcomes?

rolling two dice
toss one coin and roll one die;
10-digit phone numbers





The total number of relevant outcomes may heavily depend on whether, in each of your \(k\) stages of your experiment, the items that have already been chosen so far can still be chosen.






NoteDefinition



Sampling with replacement.
Selecting/obtaining \(k\) items from a total of \(n\) items with replacement.


Let’s start with the simpler case of \(k=1\), i.e., selecting one item out of \(n\).
Suppose you toss a six-sided die twice. You have \(6\) simple outcomes on the first roll and \(6\) possible outcomes in the second roll.
In this type of problem, there are a few things to check.
1. Is the experiment performed with replacement? Yes; if the first roll is a \(2\), nothing precludes the fact that the second roll is a \(2\) again.
2. Does the order matter? Yes; the pair \((2,5)\) corresponding to a \(2\) on the first roll and a \(5\) on the second roll is not equal to the pair \((5,2)\) corresponding to a \(5\) on the first roll and a \(2\) on the second roll. We will revisit this when we learn about permutations.






TipExample



Suppose a box contains \(6\) numbered balls; for each selection, record the number and put the selected ball back to the box. Is this sampling with or without replacement? What is the total number of possible outcomes?


(Note, the experiment where you roll two fair dice is the same experiment as one dice being independently rolled twice.)
Next, what if the sampling is done without replacement?






NoteDefinition



Sampling without replacement.
Selecting \(k\) items from a total of \(n\) items without replacement.


Here is an example. We’d like to count how many different subsets of three people can become officers of an organization of \(n=30\) people, if chosen randomly? Order doesn’t matter here (we are not interested in the exact appointments for a given candidate). The random sampling of random three officers from \(n\) people is a sampling conducted without replacement.
Here are some other examples:

Texas Holdem: 3 common cards are dealt sequentially from a deck of cards. 2 cards are dealt to each player from the same deck.
Blackjack: 2 cards are dealt to each player from the same pile of cards.
Lotto numbers are drawn sequentially.




We will learn three tools for counting. This is called combinatorics, and is an elegant branch of mathematics that we borrow from.

Permutations
Combinations
Partitions

First, we use a core counting operation called factorials.






NoteDefinition



Factorial.
Factorial \(n!\) is defined as \[n! =n\times (n-1) \times ... \times 2 \times 1.\]


A factorial is useful for counting permutations.






NoteDefinition



All permutations.
The number of distinct orderings of \(n\) elements is \(n!\).


Next, we define permutation number \(P_{n,k}\), the way to order \(k\) elements chosen from \(n\) elements; also called \(k\)-permutation.






NoteDefinition



Permutation number.
Permutation number \(P_{n,k}\) is the number of distinct orderings such that \(k\) elements are selected from \(n\) items in order, without replacement. \[P_{n,k} =   n!/(n-k)! = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2), \cdots, (n-r+1).\] Note: Order matters!


Consider the example from before. There are 30 members in a student organization and they need to choose a president, a vice-president, and a treasurer. In how many ways can this be done? The size of the \(n\) distinct elements (persons) is \(n =
30\), the number of persons to be appointed is \(r = 3\). The sampling is done without replacement (a president is chosen out of \(30\) people, then among the \(29\) people left a vice-president is chosen, and finally among the \(28\) people left a treasurer is chosen).
Does the order matter? Yes, the president is elected first, then the vice-president, and finally the treasurer (think about ‘ranking’ the 30 candidates). The number of ways in which the three positions can be assigned is therefore \(P_{30,3} = 30!/(30-3)! = 30 \cdot 29 \cdot 28 = 24360.\)
Note, the number of ways to choose \(n\) out of \(n\) elements is \(P_{n,n}\) simplifies to \(n\) factorial (\(n!\)). In this case, no choosing occurs; we only need to count the ways to order.






TipExample



Choosing officers.
Suppose a club has 25 members, a president and a secretary are to be chosen from the membership. How many distinct configurations can we have?








TipExample



Bookshelf.
Suppose you have 10 books on your bookshelf, how many ways are there to arrange all of the books?








TipExample



Birthday problem.
What is the probability that at least two of the students in STAT131 have the same birthday?
Hint: \(E=\{\)at least two of the students have the same birthday\(\}\) and we are interested in \(\mathbb{P}(E)\).


Approximate factorials Most computers cannot handle \(n!\) and arithmetic operations when \(n\) is big. The trick is to complete the arithmetic operations in log-scale and exponentiate the results in the end.
To compute \(\frac{P_{n,k}}{n^k}\), we compute \(\log(P_{n,k}) - k \log (n)\) where \(\log(P_{n,k}) = \log(n!)-\log((n-k)!) = \sum_{i=n-k+1}^n\log(i)\). Identity: \(\frac{P_{n,k}}{n^k} = e^{\log(P_{n,k}) - k \log (n) }\) where \(\log(\cdot)\) is the natural log.






NoteDefinition



Combination number.
Suppose a set has \(n\) elements, select \(k\) elements without replacement. Each subset of size \(k\) is a combination of \(n\) elements taken \(k\) at a time. The number of distinct combinations: \[C_{n,k} = \frac{P_{n,k}}{k!} = \frac{n!} {(n-k)!k!}.\] Also known as binomial coefficients \(\binom{n}{k}\). Note: Order doesn’t matter!


The combination number is used in the famed binomial theorem.






ImportantTheorem



Binomial theorem.
\[(x+y)^n = \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{k} x^ky^{n-k}.\]








TipExample



Complete square: \((x+y)^2= ?\) and \((x+y)^3= ?\).








ImportantLemma



A few frequently used properties of binomial coefficients:

\(\binom{n}{0} = \binom{n}{n} =1\),
\(\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}\).
\(\binom{n}{k} + \binom{n}{k-1} = \binom{n+1}{k}\).
Vandermonde’s identity: \[\binom{m+n}{k} = \sum_{j=0}^k\binom{m}{j} \binom{n}{k-j}.\]









TipExample



Texas Holdem.
A 5-card hand is dealt from a standard, well-shuffled 52-card deck. The hand is called a full house in poker if it consists of three cards of some rank and two cards of another rank. e.g. three \(K\)’s + two 7’s, where ordering does not matter. What is the probability of a full house?








TipExample



Blood Alleles.
The gene for human blood type consists of a pair of alleles chosen from the three alleles commonly called O, A, and B. For example, two possible combinations of alleles (called genotypes) to form a blood-type gene would be BB and AO. We will not distinguish the same two alleles in different orders, so OA represents the same genotype as AO. How many genotypes are there for blood type?








TipExample



Fair coin tossed.
A fair coin is to be tossed 10 times. Determine the probability that exactly 3 heads will occur? Also determine the probability that three or fewer heads will occur?








TipExample



Sampling without replacement.
Suppose an urn contains 15 yellow and 30 blue balls, from which 10 balls will be selected at random. What is the probability that exactly three yellow balls will be selected?


Next, suppose we want to partition a set of \(n\) elements into \(r\) subsets so that the \(i\)’th subset contains \(n_i\) elements, and \(\sum_i n_i = n\). How many ways to do this?






NoteDefinition



Partitions.
The number of ways to partition \(n\) elements into \(n_1, \cdots, n_r\) groups is \[\binom{n}{n_1,\cdots, n_r}.\] This is the multinomial coefficient.


Q: Can you see how the combinations \(C_{n,k}\) are a specific case of partitions, so that the binomial coefficient is a specific case of the multinomial coefficient?






TipExample



How many different words (even meaningless) can be obtained by rearranging the word PEPPER?

title: Lecture 1: Classical probability theory
text:
NoteDefinition



Experiment.
The experiment is any process where its possible outcomes can be identified ahead of time. An event is a well-defined set of possible outcomes of the experiment.


In the following two scenarios, the words following “the probability that” describe the event of interest.

In an experiment in which the air temperature at a certain location is to be observed every day at noon for 90 successive days, a person might want to determine the probability that the average temperature during this period will be less than some specified value.
In an experiment in which a sample of 1000 transistors is to be selected from a large shipment of similar items and each selected item is to be inspected, a person might want to determine the probability that not more than one of the selected transistors will be defective.







NoteDefinition



Sample space.
The sample space \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.








TipExample



Coin tossing.
What is the sample space of the following experiments?

Tossing a coin twice? three times?
The letter grade?
The human height (in feet) of a randomly chosen person?









NoteDefinition



Events.
Events (say, \(E\)) are sets of outcomes that are subsets of the sample space (i.e., \(E \in \Omega\)).


Events can consist of single outcome, or multiple outcomes.






TipExample



The letter grade.
If the experiment you’re conducting is taking a class, and the result is a letter grade, what are the following events?

Getting an A in the class.
Passing the course.
Failing the course.









TipExample



Two coin tosses.
If you toss a fair coin twice, what are the following events?

Getting exactly one tail.
Getting exactly one head.
Getting more heads than tails.



Note: These are discrete events, i.e. they are a collection of sample points from a discrete sample space. A discrete sample space \(\Omega\) is one that contains either a finite or countable number of distinct sample points.
In this part of the course, just assume we deal with discrete events from a discrete sample spaces. Later, we will deal with continuous sample spaces.

text:
Basic Set Theory [DS 1.1-1.4] [Lec 1]
In probability theory, the notion of an “event” is usually described in terms of a set (of outcomes). Therefore, before beginning our discussion of probability theory, we will review some basic facts about set theory.
Note to students: I will cover this as a review, but I will assume you are proficient in basic set theory (unions, intersections, de Morgan’s law, etc.).






NoteDefinition



Universal set, Set, Subset, Empty set








NoteDefinition



Venn diagram








NoteDefinition



Set operations.
There are three basic set operations:

Complement: \(A^C\),
Union: \(A \cup B\)
Intersection: \(A \cap B\)




Properties of complement

\((A^C)^C = A\)
\(\emptyset^C=\Omega\), \(\Omega ^C=\emptyset\)



Properties of union

\(A\cup B = B \cup A\),
\(A \cup A =  \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), \(A \cup A^C =  \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), \(A \cup \emptyset = \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), \(A \cup \Omega = \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\)
\(A \cup B =\rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), if \(A \subset B\).



Properties of intersection

\(A\cap B = B \cap A\),
\(A \cap A =  \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), \(A \cap A^C =  \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), \(A \cap \emptyset = \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), \(A \cap \Omega = \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\)
\(A \cap B =\rule{1cm}{0.15mm}\), if \(A \subset B\).







NoteDefinition



Disjoint.
Two sets are disjoint, if their intersection is empty.








ImportantTheorem



De Morgan’s law.
\[(A\cup B)^C = A^C \cap B^C.\] \[(A\cap B)^C = A^C \cup B^C.\]


This can be extended to the union or intersection of any \(n > 0\) sets:

\(\left(\cup_{i=1}^n A_i\right)^c=\cap_{i=1}^n A_i^c\)
\(\left(\cap_{i=1}^n A_i\right)^c=\cup_{i=1}^n A_i^c\).







ImportantTheorem



Associative properties.
\[A\cup B \cup C= (A\cup B) \cup C = A\cup (B \cup C)\] \[A\cap B \cap C= (A\cap B) \cap C = A\cap (B \cap C)\]








ImportantTheorem



Distributive properties.
\[A\cap (B \cup C)= (A\cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\] \[A\cup (B \cap C)= (A\cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\]








NoteDefinition



Partition.
The collection of sets \(\{E_i\}_{i=1}\) is a partition of \(A\), if \[A = \cup_{i=1} E_i,  \text{ and }
  E_i\cap E_j = \emptyset \text{ for all } i \neq j.\]


The collection of sets can be either finite or infinite. Also, partition is not unique. For example,

Define \(E_i = \{i\}\) for \(i=1,2,...\). Then, \(\{E_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\) is a partition of positive integers. Also there are infinitely many partitioning sets.
Define \(E_1=\{1,2\}\) and \(E_2=\{3,4,...\}\). Then, \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) is also a (finite) partition of positive integers.

A set \(A\) can always be partitioned with respect to another set \(B\) as: \[A = (A\cap B) \cup (A \cap B^C),\]
and the union of two sets can be partitioned by \(A\) and the rest: \[A \cup B =  A \cup (B \cap A^C)\]
You’ll notice that partitioning components must be disjoint.

title: Lecture 1: Classical probability theory
text:
Probability [DS 1.1, 1.2, 1.5] [Lec 1] {#sec: probability}
What is probability, and how to interpretate it? Two ways:

objective probability: long run relative frequency of a given event (e.g., seeing heads in a coin flip).
subjective probability: subjective belief in the rate of occurrence of a given event.







TipExample



What is the chance of raining tomorrow? As we cannot repeat tomorrow, the long run relative frequency interpretation is not convincing. In contrast, the subjective belief approach is more sensible.


In either case, we may use the framework in this class without inconsistency. For example, the way we’d calculate the chances of raining two days in a row would be the same, regardless of which interpretation of probability we took.
We will take the objective (frequentist) view often in this class.
For probability calculations that we might find interesting, there are three simple conditions that must be met by the collection of sets that we call events. Let’s formalize this.
In a given experiment, we must assign to each event \(A\) in the sample space \(\Omega\) a number \[\mathbb{P}(A)\] that indicates the probability that \(A\) will occur.
But not any function \(\mathbb{P}()\) will work. In order to satisfy the mathematical definition of probability, the number \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) that is assigned must satisfy three specific axioms.






NoteDefinition



Axioms of probability.
Any probability (measure) should satisfy the following axioms.

Axiom 1 (positivity): for every event \(A\), \(\mathbb{P}(A) \ge 0\).
Axiom 2 (unity): \(\mathbb{P}(\Omega) =1\).
Axiom 3 (countable additivity): For every infinite sequence of disjoint events \(A_1, A_2,...\), \[\mathbb{P}(\cup_{i=1}^\infty A_i) = \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^\infty\mathbb{P}(A_i).\]



We will continue to cover this next time.

title: Lecture 2: Probability basics, continued
text:
Let’s start with a review.
Recall an experiment from the previous lecture in which we toss a fair coin twice. If we were to repeat the experiment over and over again, what is the frequency of the occurrence of the sequence HT? What about the other sequences? What about the frequency of \(\{HT\} \cup \{TT\}\)? We need a way to measure the frequency or probability of an event.
In a given experiment, we must assign to each event \(A\) in the sample space \(\Omega\) a number \[\mathbb{P}(A)\] that indicates the probability that \(A\) will occur.
The function \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) of event \(A\) must satisfy:

Axiom 1 (positivity): for every event \(A\), \(\mathbb{P}(A) \ge 0\).
Axiom 2 (unity): \(\mathbb{P}(\Omega) =1\).
Axiom 3 (countable additivity): For every infinite sequence of disjoint events \(A_1, A_2,...\), \[\mathbb{P}(\cup_{i=1}^\infty A_i) = \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^\infty\mathbb{P}(A_i).\]

The first two are intuitive. Let’s look at the third. If you have disjoint events \(A_1\) and \(A_2\), the probability of \(A_1 \cup A_2\) occurring should be the sum of the probabilities. This simply extends to any countably infinite sequence of events \(A_1,A_2,\cdots\).






NoteDefinition



A probability measure, or simply a probability, on a sample space \(\Omega\) is a specification of numbers \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) for all events \(A\) that satisfy Axioms 1, 2, and 3.


By the definition, probability is a mapping from sets (events) to \([0,1]\). Simply put, probability is a set-valued function, mapping sets to real numbers.






TipExample



Roll one dice.
Let’s say we roll one six-sided dice, and define the probability measure to be \[\mathbb{P}(A) = \frac{\text{No. of elements in event A}}{\text{No. of elements in
      sample space}}.\] Is this a valid probability measure?


Now, assume we have a probability measure \(\mathbb{P}\). Let’s build some basic properties of probability measures.






ImportantLemma



Empty set.
Some events are impossible. For example, when a die is rolled, it is impossible to obtain a negative number. \(\mathbb{P}(\emptyset) =0\).



Proof. Proof. By Axiom 1 and Axiom 3. ◻







ImportantLemma



Finite additivity.
For every finite sequence of disjoint events \(A_1, A_2,..., A_n\), \[\mathbb{P}(\cup_{i=1}^n  A_i) = \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n \mathbb{P}(A_i).\]



Proof. Proof. By Axiom 3 and \(\mathbb{P}(\emptyset) =0\). ◻



The following properties can be shown using the axioms of probability. (What do these properties mean, in plain words? Take \(A\) to be the event that it rains tomorrow.)

Complement: \(\mathbb{P}(A^C) = 1-\mathbb{P}(A)\).
Inclusion: If \(A \subset B\), then \(\mathbb{P}(A) \le \mathbb{P}(B)\).
Regularity: for every event \(A\), \(\mathbb{P}(A) \in [0,1]\).


Proof. Proof. For practice, prove these using the probability Axioms. ◻

Probability on finite sample spaces [DS 1.6] [Lec 2]
In classical probability theory, sample spaces are often finite—the number of outcomes is finite. For instance, dice rolling, drawing a few cards from a deck of cards, etc..
A general probability theory can be established for the experiments with equally likely outcomes.






NoteDefinition



Equally likely outcomes.
Suppose \(\Omega = \{\omega_i\}_{i=1}^N\), \(\mathbb{P}(\omega_i) = \frac{1}{N}\) for \(i=1,..,N\).


With equally likely outcomes, the probability calculation is simply counting. The measure \(\mathbb{P}\) is called the counting measure.






ImportantTheorem



For the finite sample space \(\Omega\) with equally likely outcomes, the probability of event \(E \subset \Omega\) is \[\mathbb{P}(E) = \frac{|E|}{|\Omega|},\] where \(|E|\) denotes the number of outcomes in \(E\).








TipExample



Tossing coins.
Suppose three fair coins are tossed simultaneously. What is the probability of obtaining exactly two heads?









TipExample



Roll two fair dice.
Two fair dice are rolled. What are the equally likely outcomes? Which is more likely:

sum is 11 v.s. sum is 12?









TipExample



Genetics.
Inherited traits in humans are determined by material in specific locations on chromosomes. There are pairs of chromosomes that the child inherits from the parents. The material in those two locations make up a gene, and can be either A or a. (These are called alleles). Each distinct combination of alleles is called a genotype.
For example, a parent who has Aa can give the the child both A and a. A parent who has aa can only give a. We also consider Aa and aA to be the same. Also assume that all possible results of the parents contributing pairs of alleles are equally likely.

If the parents are both Aa, what are the possible genotypes? (in other words, what is the sample space?)
What is the probability associated with those genotypes?
Next, if one parent is Aa and the other is aa, find the genotypes for an offspring. What is the sample space?

title: Lecture 4: Conditional probability
text:
When you have multiple random phenoma, they rarely have nothing to do with each other. They are often dependent on a common factor, or one is affecting the other, directly or indirectly.
Say a random person is selected from the population; compare the following scenarios:

COVID infection rate
COVID infection rate if the person is fully vaccinated.

The two probabilities should clearly be different. When more information (“vaccinated”) is available, the probability calculation should reflect it.






NoteDefinition



Conditional probability.
The probability of event \(A\) given event \(B\) has occurred is denoted as \(\mathbb{P}(A|B)\). If \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), \[\mathbb{P}(A|B) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.\]


We can interpretate \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) as the “prior” probability of \(A\) without any other information. In contrast, we interpretate \(\mathbb{P}(A|B)\) as the “posterior” probability of \(A\) given \(B\) has occurred.
Let’s try this out on an example.






TipExample



By using a certain prescription drug, there is a 10% chance of experiencing headaches, a 15% chance of experiencing nausea, and a 5% chance of experiencing both headaches and nausea. What is the probability that you will experience an headache given that you feel nauseous after taking the prescription drug?


Note, the conditional probability \(\mathbb{P}(\cdot|B)\) with respect to an event B (with \(\mathbb{P}(B) > 0\)) is a proper probability measure, therefore the three axioms of probability that we discussed in Lecture hold for \(\mathbb{P}(\cdot|B)\) as well. When it comes to standard computations, \(\mathbb{P}(\cdot|B)\) has the same properties as \(\mathbb{P}(\cdot)\). For instance, for disjoint events \(A_1,A_2 \in \Omega\) we have \[P(A_1 \cup A_2|B) = P(A_1|B) + P(A_2|B).\] Neat!
Next, we can relate the joint probability \(\mathbb{P}(A \cap B)\) to event \(B\) using the following rule.






ImportantLemma



Multiplicative rule.
Let \(A,B\) be two events. If \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), \[\mathbb{P}(A\cap B) = \mathbb{P}(A|B) {\mathbb{P}(B)}.\] Further, let \(A_i\) be a sequence of events such that \(\mathbb{P}(\cap_{i=1}^{n-1}A_i) >0\). Then, \[\mathbb{P}(\cap_{i=1}^{n} A_i) = \mathbb{P}(A_1)\mathbb{P}(A_2|A_1)
  \mathbb{P}(A_3|A_1\cap A_2)...\mathbb{P}(A_n|\cap_{i=1}^{n-1}A_i) .\]



Proof. Proof. Proof by induction. First verify the case \(n=2\) holds. Then suppose the case \(n-1\) holds, and show the case \(n\) also holds. ◻

Next, the Bayes rule is about the reversal of the two events \(B|A\); how does it relate to \(A|B\)? Let’s see this next.






ImportantTheorem



Bayes rule.
Let \(A,B\) be two events. If \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), \[\mathbb{P}(A|B) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(B|A)\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)},\] where the denominator \(\mathbb{P}(B)=\mathbb{P}(B|A)\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B|A^c)\mathbb{P}(A^c)\).



Proof. Proof. By definition of the conditional probability and the multiplicative rule. ◻

We will revisit the Bayes rule more in detail in the next section.
The law of total probability allows us to extend the Bayes rule to multiple events \(B_1, \cdots, B_k\) so we can relate \(B_j|A\) to \(A | B_j\).






ImportantTheorem



The law of total probability.
Suppose events \(\{B_j \}\) form a partition of the sample space \(\Omega\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B_j)>0\) for all \(j=1,...,k\). Then, for every event \(A \subset \Omega\), \[\mathbb{P}(A) = \sum\nolimits_{j=1}^k\mathbb{P}(B_j) \mathbb{P}(A|B_j).\]



Proof. Proof. By the definition of partition and the multiplicative rule. ◻

There is a “conditional” version of the law of total probability, which simply uses \(\mathbb{P}(\cdot)\) with \(\mathbb{P}(\cdot | C)\) for some other event \(C\): \[\mathbb{P}(A|C) = \sum\nolimits_{j=1}^k\mathbb{P}(B_j|C) \mathbb{P}(A|B_j\cap C).\]






TipExample



Rare disease.
We are dealing with a rare disease with an overall disease rate: \(\mathbb{P}(D) = 1\%\) where \(D\) is the event that a person has the disease. There is a diagnostic test whose accuracy 95%. Denoting as \(T\) the event that the test is positive, we also know that \(\mathbb{P}(T|D) = 0.95\). We also know that \(\mathbb{P}(T|D^C) = 0.1\). (What are these two events, in words?)

Suppose John Doe is diagnosed with positive. What is the probability that he has the disease?
Suppose John Doe is diagnosed with negative. What is the probability that he does not have the disease?
Suppose John Doe is diagnosed with negative. What is the probability that he does have the disease?
