title: Lecture 4: Conditional probability
text:
Bayes rule revisited [DS 2.3] [Lec 4]
(This section is meant for self-study. Also try the examples and practice problems in DS section 2.3.)
Knowing conditional probability, we can derive a useful theorem to calculate the reversed conditional probabilities. Say we have disjoint events \(B_1, \cdots, B_k\). Also take another event \(A\). If \(\mathbb{P}(A|B_i)\) is available for each \(i\), then Bayes theorem is a useful formula for computing the conditional probabilities of the events \(B_i\) given \(A\).






ImportantTheorem



Bayes’ rule.
Let the events \(B_1, \ldots, B_k\) form a partition of the space \(S\) such that \(\mathbb{P}\left(B_j\right)>0\) for \(j=1, \ldots, k\), and let \(A\) be an event such that \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\). Then, for \(i=1, \ldots, k\), \[\mathbb{P}\left(B_i \mid A\right)=\frac{\mathbb{P}\left(B_i\right) \mathbb{P}\left(A \mid B_i\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^k \mathbb{P}\left(B_j\right) \mathbb{P}\left(A \mid B_j\right)} .\]


Let us prove this. By the definition of conditional probability, \[\mathbb{P}\left(B_i \mid A\right)=\frac{\mathbb{P}\left(B_i \cap A\right)}{\mathbb{P}(A)} .\] The numerator is equal to \(\mathbb{P}\left(B_i \cap A\right)\) by the Multiplicative rule. Similarly, the denominator is equal to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\), which is the sum of the probabilities of the partitions \(B_i \cap A, i = 1,\cdots, k\).






TipExample



Test for a Disease..
Suppose that you are walking down the street and notice that the Department of Public Health is giving a free medical test for a certain disease. The test is 90 percent reliable in the following sense: If a person has the disease, there is a probability of 0.9 that the test will give a positive response; whereas, if a person does not have the disease, there is a probability of only 0.1 that the test will give a positive response. Data indicate that your chances of having the disease are only 1 in 10,000. However, since the test costs you nothing, and is fast and harmless, you decide to stop and take the test. A few days later you learn that you had a positive response to the test. Now, what is the probability that you have the disease?


Side note: The underlined question is a prototype of the question for which Bayes’ rule was designed. We have at least two disjoint events (“you have the disease” and “you do not have the disease”) about which we are uncertain, and we learn a piece of information (the result of the test) that tells us something about the uncertain events. Then we need to know how to revise the probabilities of the events in the light of the information we learned.
At a glance, we may feel that this probability should be about 0.9. However, this feeling completely ignores the small probability of 0.0001 that you had the disease before taking the test.
We shall let \(B_1\) denote the event that you have the disease, and let \(B_2\) denote the event that you do not have the disease. The events \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) form a partition. Also, let \(A\) denote the event that the response to the test is positive. The event \(A\) is information we will learn that tells us something about the partition elements.
Then, by Bayes’ theorem,
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{P} \left(B_1 \mid A\right) & =\frac{\mathbb{P}\left(A \mid B_1\right) \mathbb{P}\left(B_1\right)}{\mathbb{P}\left(A \mid B_1\right) \mathbb{P}\left(B_1\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(A \mid B_2\right) \mathbb{P}\left(B_2\right)} \\
                              & =\frac{(0.9)(0.0001)}{(0.9)(0.0001)+(0.1)(0.9999)}=0.00090.
\end{aligned}\]
Thus, the conditional probability that you have the disease given the test result is approximately only 1 in 1000. Of course, this conditional probability is approximately 9 times as great as the probability was before you were tested, but even the conditional probability is quite small.
Another way to explain this result is as follows: Only one person in every 10,000 actually has the disease, but the test gives a positive response for approximately one person in every 10. Hence, the number of positive responses is approximately 1000 times the number of persons who actually have the disease. In other words, out of every 1000 persons for whom the test gives a positive response, only one person actually has the disease.
This example illustrates not only the use of Bayes’ theorem but also the importance of taking into account all of the information available in a problem.

title: Lecture 4: Conditional probability
text:
Independent events [DS 2.2] [Lec 4]
The event \(A\) is said to be independent of event \(B\) if the occurrence of the event B does not alter the chance that the event A happens. Made formally, this is how independence is defined:






NoteDefinition



Two independent events.
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if \[\mathbb{P}(A \cap B) = \mathbb{P}(A) \mathbb{P}(B).\] Write \(A\perp B\).


For example, imagine flipping two different fair coins. Assume the outcomes (heads and tail) are equally likely: \(A= \{\text{first try = }T\}\), and \(B= \{\text{second try = }T\}\). Then \(A \perp B\); we understand this intuitively.
In fact, assuming that \(P(B) >0\), we easily see that this is equivalent to \[P(A|B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B) = P(A)P(B)/P(B) = P(A),\] i.e. the occurrence of the event B does not alter the chance that the event A happens.
Furthermore, assuming that also \(P(A) > 0\), we see that \(P(A|B) = P(A)\) is equivalent to \(P(B|A) = P(B)\) (independence is a symmetric relation!).
Let’s try an example where we recognize independence from known probabilities of events.






TipExample



Take the following table of probabilities






\(B\)
\(B^C\)




\(A\)
0
0.2


\(A^C\)
0.4
0.4




Are the events A and B independent? Justify your answer.


For multiple events, the definition of independence is trickier. First, all events can be independent of each other:






NoteDefinition



(Mutually) Independent.
For multiple events \(A_j\), mutually independence: for any subset \(\{i_1,...,i_\ell\} \subset \{1,...,n\}\), \[\mathbb{P}(A_{i_1} \cap A_{i_2}... \cap A_{i_\ell} ) = \mathbb{P}(A_{i_1}) ...\mathbb{P}(A_{i_\ell}).\]


Also, when only pairs of events are independent of each other, we call this pairwise independence:






NoteDefinition



Pairwise independence.
For multiple events \(A_j\), pairwise independence: for every \(\{i,j\} \subset \{1,...,n\}\), \[\mathbb{P}(A_{i} \cap A_{j}) = \mathbb{P}(A_{i})\mathbb{P}(A_{j}).\]


Of course, pairwise independent is weaker than (mutually) independent.






TipExample



Mutually independent but not pairwise independent.
Suppose a fair coin is tossed twice. Define the following three events:

\(A=\{H \text{ on first toss.}\},\)
\(B=\{T \text{ on second toss.}\},\)
\(C=\{\text{Both tosses are the same.}\},\)

Are the events mutually independent? Pairwise independent? Prove this.


Here are some properties:

If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, then their complements are also independent.
\(\Omega\) and \(\emptyset\) are independent with any event.

Try to prove these on your own time!
Warning: Independence and Disjoint are not the same.
Two events being disjoint simply means that they do not share any jointly occurring elements. For instance, in a single coin flip example, \(A= \{H\}\) and \(B=\{T\}\) are disjoint events, but \(A\) gives perfect knowledge of \(B\), as we know that \(P(A|B) = 0\) and \(P(A|B^C) = 1\), so that \(P(A|B) \neq P(A) = 1/2\).

Finite union

Next, we learn about a formula to calculate the probability of the union of any \(n\) events. You have already seen a version of this for two events \(A\) and \(B\), where \(P(A \cup B) = \underline{\hspace{30mm}}\).






ImportantLemma



Finite union.
For every \(n\) events \(A_1,..,A_n\), \(P(\cup_{i=1}^n A_i)\) is \[\sum \nolimits_{i=1}^n\mathbb{P}(A_i ) -     \sum \nolimits _{i<j}^n\mathbb{P}(A_i\cap A_j )
  +    \sum \nolimits _{i<j<k}^n\mathbb{P}(A_i\cap A_j\cap A_k ) +...+
  (-1)^{n+1}\mathbb{P}(A_1 \cap ...\cap A_n).\]



Proof. Proof. Proof by induction. ◻

Using this lemma, we can solve the famous collector’s problem.






TipExample



The Collector’s Problem.
Randomly throw \(n\) balls into \(r\) boxes, what is the probability that every box contains at least one ball? Equivalently, sample \(n\) cards with replacement from \(r\) distinct cards, what is the probability of obtaining a complete set? 1


Lastly, we are now equipped to talk about another ‘parallel’ concept to independence.






NoteDefinition



Two conditional independent events.
Conditional on event \(C\) (such that \(P(C) > 0\)), the events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if \[\mathbb{P}(A \cap B |C) = \mathbb{P}(A|C) \mathbb{P}(B|C).\] We will write this as \(A \perp B | C\).


This implies that \(P(A | B \cap C) = P(A | C)\). We will prove this in our homework.
Here is an example using conditional independence.






TipExample



Two-stage coin flip experiment.
There is a jar of coins, which are manufactured poorly and have wildly different probabilities of getting a heads. We will draw a coint from the jar, then flip that same coin twice.
Let the event \(C\) be \(\{\text{the coin is biased, such that } \mathbb{P}(\text{Tail in one draw}) = 1/3\}\). What is the probability you will see two heads given that the coin is biased?


Conditional independence does not imply nor is it implied by independence.
Independence does not imply conditional independence. Toss two coins. Let \(H_1\) the even that the first toss is H and \(H_2\) the event that the second toss is \(H\). Let \(D\) the even that the two tosses are different. \(H_1\) and \(H_2\) are clearly independent but \(P\left(H_1 \mid D\right)=P\left(H_2 \mid D\right)=1 / 2\) and \(P\left(H_1 \cap H_2 \mid D\right)=0\).
Conditional independence does not imply independence. We have two coins, a blue one and a red one. For the blue coin the probability of \(H\) is 0.99 and for the red coin it is 0.01 . A coin is chosen at random and then tossed twice. Let \(B\) the event that the blue coin is selected, \(R\) the event that the red coin is selected. Let \(H_1\) and \(H_2\) the events that the first and second toss is \(H\). By the law of total probability
\[P\left(H_1\right)=P\left(H_1 \mid B\right) P(B)+P\left(H_1 \mid R\right) P(R)=1 / 2 .\]
Similarly \(P\left(H_2\right)=1 / 2\). But, using again the law of total probability,
\[P\left(H_1 \cap H_2\right)=P\left(H_1 \cap H_2 \mid B\right) P(B)+P\left(H_1
  \cap H_2 \mid R\right) P(R)=1 / 2 \cdot 0.99^2+1 / 2 \cdot 0.01^2 \approx 1 /
2\]
which is different than \(P\left(H_1\right) P\left(H_2\right)=1 / 4\).

title: Lecture 6: Random variables cont’d
text:
Here are some additional important discrete random variables:

Bernoulli and Binomial distribution.
The Negative Binomial distribution (and the geometric distribution; DS section 5.5).
The Poisson distribution (from DS section 5.4)

Make sure to read chapter 5 (“special distributions”) for more practice. Also see the Appendix table of distributions for a more exhaustive list; this will be especially useful once we learn about moments of these distributions.
We briefly describe a few of these important discrete distributions.
Suppose you have an infinite sequence of independent Bernoulli trials (i.e. coin flips) with probability \(p\) of success. You will continue the trials until the \(r\)’th success occurs. (Slot machines, anyone?)
The number \(X\) of the failures before you stop is distributed as a Negative Binomial random variable.






NoteDefinition



Negative Binomial distribution.
A random variable \(X\) has the Negative Binomial distribution with parameters \(0<p<1\) and \(r\) (\(r = 0,1,\cdots\)) if the pmf of \(X\) is as follows: \[f(x \mid r, p)=
  \begin{cases}\left(\begin{array}{c}r+x-1 \\
                       x\end{array}\right) p^r(1-p)^x & \text {
                                                        for }
                                                        x=0,1,2,
                                                        \ldots
    \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}\] We write \(X \sim NB(r, p)\).








TipExample



Defective Parts.. Suppose that a machine produces parts that can be either good or defective. Let \(X_i = 1\) if the \(i\)’th part is defective and \(X_i = 0\) otherwise. Assume that the parts are good or defective independently of each other with \(\mathbb{P}(X_i= 1) = p\) for all \(i\). An inspector observes the parts produced by this machine until she sees four defectives. Let \(X\) be the number of good parts observed by the time that the fourth defective is observed. What is the distribution of \(X\)?


A geometric distribution is the special case where \(r=1\). Say you are waiting for the first day it will rain, where the daily probability of raining is \(p\). Then the total number of days it will take to rain is \(X\).
Next, we will study the Poisson random variable and distribution.






NoteDefinition



Poisson distribution.
A random variable \(X\) has the Poisson distribution with mean parameter \(\lambda>0\) if the pmf of \(X\) is as follows: \[f(x\mid \lambda) = \mathbb{P}(X=x) = \begin{cases}
                      \frac{\lambda^{x} e^{-\lambda}}{x!} & \text{ for } x=0,1,\cdots,\\
                      0 & \text{ otherwise.}
                    \end{cases}\] For such a random variable, we write \(X \sim Poiss(\lambda)\).


Q: Why is it called a “mean” parameter?
A Poisson random variable (we also say a Poisson-distributed RV) is apt for describing the number of occurrences of an “arrival” process for which (1) arrivals are independent of each other, and (2) the average time between arrivals stays the same. \(\lambda\) is the expected number of occurrences in a unit amount of time. Classic examples are phone calls, earthquakes, and bus arrivals.






TipExample



Customer arrivals. A store owner believes that customers arrive at her store at a rate of \(4.5\) customers per hour on average. She might want to find the distribution of the actual number \(X\) of customers who will arrive during a particular one-hour period later in the day. \(X \sim Poiss(\lambda = 4.5)\). What is the probability that \(3\) customers will arrive in the next hour?


Next, we are interested not only in the number of customers that arrive in the one-hour period, but also in how many customers arrive in the next hour after that period. Let \(Y\) be the number of customers that arrive in the second hour, and model \(Y\) as another Poisson random variable with mean \(4.5\). What is the distribution of \(X+Y\)?
In order to answer this, we need to learn about sums of Poisson. Poisson random variables have the convenient property of being closed to summation.






ImportantTheorem



Poisson sums.
If the random variables \(X_1, \cdots, X_k\) are independent 1 and if \(X_i\) has the Poisson distribution with mean \(\lambda_i (i=1,\cdots,k)\), then the sum \(X = X_1 +\cdots +X_k\) has the Poisson distribution with mean \(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_k\).


Proof: We will soon learn about moment generating functions, to prove the general case. Let’s prove the \(k=2\) case.
\[\begin{aligned} P(X+Y=k) &=\sum_{i=0}^k P(X+Y=k, X=i)
                          =\sum_{i=0}^k P(Y=k-i, X=i)
                          =\sum_{i=0}^k P(Y=k-i) P(X=i) \\
                          &=\sum_{i=0}^k e^{-\lambda_1} \frac{\lambda_1^{k-i}}{(k-i) !}
                            e^{-\lambda_2} \frac{\lambda_2^i}{i
                            !}  
                          =e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)} \frac{1}{k !} \sum_{i=0}^k
                            \frac{k !}{i !(k-i) !}  \lambda_1^{k-i} \lambda_2^i
                          =e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)} \frac{1}{k !}
                            \sum_{i=0}^k\left(\begin{array}{l}k \\
                                                i\end{array}\right) \lambda_1^{k-i}
                            \lambda_2^i \\
                          &=\frac{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^k}{k !} \cdot
                            e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)}
\end{aligned}\]






TipExample



Arrivals in two hours instead of one.
Now, returning to the store example, we would also say that \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent because we have been assuming that arrivals (in disjoint time intervals) are independent. Then, we now know that \(Z=X + Y\) would have the Poisson distribution with mean \(4.5 + 4.5 = 9\). What is the probability that at least \(12\) customers will arrive in the entire two-hour period?
We can compute this using probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(Z \ge 12) = 0.1970\) easily using a computer. (In R, the command is 1-ppois(11, 9), which calculates \(1-\mathbb{P}(Z \le 11)\).)
(If we want to be old school, we can go to DS book’s “Table of Poisson Probabilities” and see the column with the parameter \(\lambda = 9\).)

title: Lecture 8: Cumulative distribution functions
text:
So far we’ve made a clear distinction between continuous RVs (for which pdfs are the probability density) and discrete RVs (for which pmfs are the density).
We now introduce one concept – cumulative distribution functions (cdfs) – that can serve as general-purpose descriptions of distributions/random variables.






NoteDefinition



Cumulative Distribution Function.
For all \(x\in \bR\), the cumulative distribution function \(F\) is the function \[F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X \le x).\]


discrete continuous random variables \(X\) can be defined using a cdf.
Suppose \(X\) has pmf \(f(\cdot)\), then its cdf is: \[F(x) = \sum\nolimits_{y \le x} f(y).\]
Also, suppose \(X\) has pdf \(f(\cdot)\), then its cdf is: \[F(x) = \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^x f(y)dy.\]






TipExample



Find and sketch the cdfs of the following random variables.

Bernoulli(\(p\)).
Uniform distribution on \([0,1]\).



Conversely, \(f(x) = \frac{d}{dx}F(x)\) at all \(x\) where \(F\) is differentiable.
(note the resemblance to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.)
(Also note that sometimes we will include the subscript \(X\) in cdfs (\(F_X\)) or pdfs or pmfs (\(f_X\)).)






TipExample



Find the pdf of the following cdf: \[F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } x<0 \\ x^{2 / 3} & \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 1 & \text { for } x>1\end{cases}\]
(Hint: draw the cdf. What are all the differentiable points?)


Next, here are some properties of cdfs:

(1) A cdf is non-decreasing: \(F(x_1) \le F(x_2)\) if \(x_1<x_2\).
(2) A cdf’s limits are at \(\pm \infty\).
(3) A cdf is always continuous from the right: \(F(x) =F(x^+)\) for all \(x \in \bR\).

Here we pause and emphasize that a cdf need not be continuous. In fact, the value of \(F(x)\) may jump at any finite or countable number of points.
You can calculate probabilities regarding random variable \(X\) directly from its cdf \(F\) in the following ways:

(1) For every \(x \in \bR\), \(\mathbb{P}(X>x) = 1- F(x)\).
(2) For all \(x_1<x_2\), \(\mathbb{P}( x_1 <X \le x_2) = F(x_2) - F(x_1)\).
(3) For every \(x \in \bR\), \(\mathbb{P}(X<x) = F(x^-)\).
(4) For every \(x \in \bR\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) = F(x) - F(x^-)\).







TipExample



Take a random variable \(X\) whose cdf \(F\) is as follows. 1

\(\mathbb{P}(X<0)\)

\(\mathbb{P}(0 \leq X \leq 3)\)

Next, we learn about an alternative representation of a random variable’s distribution, the quantile function. A quantile function is roughly the inverse of the cdf.






NoteDefinition



Quantile.
For \(p \in (0,1)\), \(p-\)quantile of \(X\), denoted as \(F^{-1}(p)\), is the smallest value \(x\) such that \[F(x) \ge p.\] a.k.a. \(100p\) percentile of \(X\)


median.

One might ask: when is a quantile an exact inverse of a cdf?






ImportantTheorem



When the random variable \(X\) is continuous, the quantile function \(F^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(F\).

NoteDefinition



Frequently used quantiles.
The 1/2 quantile or the 50th percentile of a distribution is called its median. The 1/4 quantile or 25th percentile is the lower quartile. The 3/4 quantile or 75th percentile is called the upper quartile.


The median is the number divides the distribution in half as closely as is possible.
(And if there are ties, take the middle value).
A median of a distribution is important because it helps summarize the distribution of a random variable, answering the question: what is the most “representative” value?






TipExample

title: Lecture 8: Cumulative distribution functions
text:
So far we’ve made a clear distinction between continuous RVs (for which pdfs are the probability density) and discrete RVs (for which pmfs are the density).
We now introduce one concept – cumulative distribution functions (cdfs) – that can serve as general-purpose descriptions of distributions/random variables.






NoteDefinition



Cumulative Distribution Function.
For all \(x\in \bR\), the cumulative distribution function \(F\) is the function \[F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X \le x).\]


discrete continuous random variables \(X\) can be defined using a cdf.
Suppose \(X\) has pmf \(f(\cdot)\), then its cdf is: \[F(x) = \sum\nolimits_{y \le x} f(y).\]
Also, suppose \(X\) has pdf \(f(\cdot)\), then its cdf is: \[F(x) = \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^x f(y)dy.\]






TipExample



Find and sketch the cdfs of the following random variables.

Bernoulli(\(p\)).
Uniform distribution on \([0,1]\).



Conversely, \(f(x) = \frac{d}{dx}F(x)\) at all \(x\) where \(F\) is differentiable.
(note the resemblance to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.)
(Also note that sometimes we will include the subscript \(X\) in cdfs (\(F_X\)) or pdfs or pmfs (\(f_X\)).)






TipExample



Find the pdf of the following cdf: \[F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } x<0 \\ x^{2 / 3} & \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 1 & \text { for } x>1\end{cases}\]
(Hint: draw the cdf. What are all the differentiable points?)


Next, here are some properties of cdfs:

(1) A cdf is non-decreasing: \(F(x_1) \le F(x_2)\) if \(x_1<x_2\).
(2) A cdf’s limits are at \(\pm \infty\).
(3) A cdf is always continuous from the right: \(F(x) =F(x^+)\) for all \(x \in \bR\).

Here we pause and emphasize that a cdf need not be continuous. In fact, the value of \(F(x)\) may jump at any finite or countable number of points.
You can calculate probabilities regarding random variable \(X\) directly from its cdf \(F\) in the following ways:

(1) For every \(x \in \bR\), \(\mathbb{P}(X>x) = 1- F(x)\).
(2) For all \(x_1<x_2\), \(\mathbb{P}( x_1 <X \le x_2) = F(x_2) - F(x_1)\).
(3) For every \(x \in \bR\), \(\mathbb{P}(X<x) = F(x^-)\).
(4) For every \(x \in \bR\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) = F(x) - F(x^-)\).

Next, we learn about an alternative representation of a random variable’s distribution, the quantile function. A quantile function is roughly the inverse of the cdf.






NoteDefinition



Quantile.
For \(p \in (0,1)\), \(p-\)quantile of \(X\), denoted as \(F^{-1}(p)\), is the smallest value \(x\) such that \[F(x) \ge p.\] a.k.a. \(100p\) percentile of \(X\)

Frequently used quantiles.
The 1/2 quantile or the 50th percentile of a distribution is called its median. The 1/4 quantile or 25th percentile is the lower quartile. The 3/4 quantile or 75th percentile is called the upper quartile.


The median is the number divides the distribution in half as closely as is possible.
(And if there are ties, take the middle value).
A median of a distribution is important because it helps summarize the distribution of a random variable, answering the question: what is the most “representative” value?

Often, we start with a joint distribution of two RVs and we then want to find the distribution of just one of them.
The distribution of one random variable \(X\) computed from a joint distribution is also called the marginal distribution of \(X\). Each random variable will have a marginal cdf as well as a marginal pdf or pmf.
First, how do we learn about the distribution of \(X\) from the joint cdf \(F(x,y)\)? The marginal cdf of \(X\) is \[F_X(x) = \lim\nolimits_{y \to \infty}F(x,y).\]
1. If \((X,Y)\) is continuous, the marginal pdf of \(X\) is \[f_X(x)  = \frac{d}{dx}F_X(x)

\[f_X(x) = \int_y f(x,y) \text{\; for all\;} x.\]
and the marginal pdf \(f_Y\) of \(Y\) can be obtained by: \[f_Y(y) = \sum_x f(x,y) \text{\; for \;}-\infty < y < \infty.\]

Independent Random Variables [DS 3.6] [Lec 10]
For a pair of events \(A\) and \(B\), they are independent if and only if \[P(A\cap B) =P(A) P(B).\] We will use the independence of events to define the independence of random variables.






NoteDefinition



two random variables are independent.
Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, denoted as \(X \perp Y\), if \[\mathbb{P}(X\in A, Y\in B) = \mathbb{P}(X\in A) \mathbb{P}(Y\in B)\] holds for all \(A\) and \(B\).


Let \(A=(-\infty,x]\) and \(B=(-\infty,y]\), then by definition, \[F(x,y) = F_X(x)F_Y(y).\] Since this holds for any \(x\) and \(y\), the implication is: the independence of \(X\) and \(Y\) implies the factorization of joint cdf into the product of the marginal cdf’s. In fact, the reverse direction also holds.






ImportantTheorem



Factorization of joint cdf.
 \(X \perp Y\) if and only if for all \(x,y \in \R\), \[F(x,y) = F_X(x)F_Y(y)\]


Next, the product of pdfs (or pmfs) must also equal the joint pdf or pmf (or pdf/pmf) for independent random variables.






ImportantTheorem



Factorization.
 If \(X\) and \(Y\) have joint pdf, joint pmf, or joint pmf/pdf \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\), then \[X \perp Y \Leftrightarrow
  f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y), \forall x,y \text{ in their supports}\]


Let us see this in an example.






TipExample



A carnival game consists of rolling a fair die, tossing a fair coin two times, and recording both outcomes. Let \(Y\) stand for the number on the die, and let \(X\) stand for the number of heads in the two tosses.

Are random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) independent?
What is the marginal distribution of \(X\)? Of \(Y?\)
Populate the following table of probabilities






The factorization theorem makes it easier to recognize independence from \(f\). If you find that \(f\) partitions into two parts – one with only \(x\) in it, and another with only \(y\) – then the two random variables are independent.






ImportantTheorem



Factorization.
If \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) satisfies \[f_{X,Y}(x,y) =h(x)g(y)\] for all \(x,y \in \bR\), where \(h(\cdot)\) and \(g(\cdot)\) are two univariate functions, then \(X\perp Y\).


(Note, [thm:ind-pdf] is a special case of this, by letting \(h_X(x)=f_X(x)\) and \(h_Y(y) = f_Y(y)\), so that \(f(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y).\))






TipExample



Examine the following joint pdfs \(f\) and determine if \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

(a) \(f(x,y) = cx^2y^2 \cdot \mathbbm{1}_{x^2+y^2\le 1}.\)
(b) \(f(x,y) = c \mathbbm{1}_{x^2 \le 1, y^2\le 1}.\)
(c) \(f(x,y) = c e^{ - x-2y} \cdot \mathbbm{1}_{x\ge 0, y\ge 0}.\)



(Hint: When the support of \((X,Y)\) have boundaries that are curved or not parallel to the coordinate axes, you cannot factorize \(f(x,y)\). All independent RVs have rectangular (even if unbounded) support!)
Lastly, any functions (or transformations) of independent random variables are also independent.






ImportantTheorem



If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(g(X)\) and \(h(Y)\) are independent for any function \(g\) and \(h\).

Conditional Distributions [DS 3.6] [Lec 10]
Recall conditional probability \[P(A|B) =\frac{P(A\cap B) }{P(B)}.\] We generalize the concept of conditional probability to conditional distributions. Recall that distributions are just collections of probabilities of events determined by random variables. Conditional distributions will be the probabilities of events determined by some random variables conditional on events determined by other random variables.
Let us start by defining a conditional probability in terms of discrete random variables.






NoteDefinition



Conditional pmf.
 The conditional pmf is \[f_{X|Y}(x|y) = \mathbb{P}(X=x|Y=y) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},\] provided \(f_Y(y)>0\).


A conditional pmf \(f_{X|Y}(x | y)\) is a valid probability mass function of \(x\). Also, the conditional probability of an event \(X\in E\) can be calculated as: \[P(X\in E|Y=y) = \sum_{x\in E}f_{X|Y}(x|y) .\]
(We can check for ourselves in the next example!)

With the joint pmf, we can answer the following questions.

What is the probability of a car being stolen?
What is the probability of a Brand 3 car being stolen?
Given a car is stolen, what is the probability of the stolen car is Brand \(k\)?



Next, we introduce conditional probabilities of continuous random variables.






NoteDefinition



Conditional pdf.
 The conditional pdf is \[f_{X|Y}(x|y) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},\] if \(f\) is the joint pdf provided \(f_Y(y)>0\).


Using this, conditional probability of \(X \in E\) for any set \(E\) can be computed as:
\[\mathbb{P}(X\in E|Y=y) = \int _{E} f_{X|Y}(x|y) dx.\]
That is, for each fixed value of \(Y=y\), \(f_{X|Y}(x|y)\) is a valid pdf in \(x\). 1

  <\infty)\). Find \(f_{X|Y}(x|y)\).

NoteDefinition



Conditional pmf or pdf from Mixed Distributions.
Let \(X\) be discrete and let \(Y\) be continuous with joint pmf/pdf \(f\). Then the conditional pmf of \(X\) given \(Y= y\) is defined by [eq:condit-pmf], and the conditional pdf of \(Y\) given \(X= x\) is defined by [eq:condit-pdf]. 2








TipExample



Suppose that a machine produces defective and nondefective parts, but we do not know what defection rate (the proportion of defective parts). Let \(P\) stand for the unknown proportion of defective parts among all possible parts produced by the machine. (If we were to learn that \(P=p\), we might be willing to say that the parts were independent of each other and each had probability \(p\) of being defective.) Let us say that if \(n\) items will be examined, \(X\) is the number of items that would be defective.

(a) What is the conditional pdf of \(X\) given \(P=p\)?
(b) What is the joint pmf/pdf of \(X\) and \(P\)?
(c) What is the conditional pdf of \(P\) given \(X=x\)?



For conditional distributions, similar conclusions to those of conditional probability also hold.
Let’s say that \(X\) and \(Y\) are random variables such that \(X\) has pmf or pdf \(f_X\), and \(Y\) has pmf or pdf \(f_Y\). Then, the joint pdf or joint pmf (or if it is a mixed scenario, a pmf/pdf) \(f(\cdot, \cdot)\) is defined as follows:






ImportantTheorem



Multiplication rule.
\[f_{(X,Y)}(x,y)=f_{X|Y}(x|y)f_Y(y) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_X(x).\]








TipExample



Suppose \(X, Y\) are independent random variables with distribution \(\text{Unif}(0,1)\). Let \(Z=\lfloor{X/Y}\rfloor\) be the floor of the ratio \(X/Y\). Show the probability \[\mathbb{P}(Z \text{ is an odd number}) = \log(2)/2.\] (Hint: use the alternating harmonic series \(\sum\nolimits^\infty_{k=1}\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} = \log(2).\))


Next, we learn about the Law of total probability and the Bayes theorem, but for random variables \(X\) and \(Y\).






ImportantTheorem



Law of total probability.
Suppose \(Y\) is continuous, \[f_X(x) = \int  f_{(X,Y)}(x,y) dy = \int  f_{X|Y}(x|y)f_Y(y) dy .\] Suppose \(Y\) is discrete, \[f_X(x) = \sum_y  f_{(X,Y)}(x,y)  = \sum_y  f_{X|Y}(x|y)f_Y(y)  .\]


Using this, we revisit the Bayes theorem.






ImportantTheorem



Bayes theorem for random variables.
\[f_{X|Y}(x,y) = \frac{f_{Y|X}(y|x) f_X(x) }{f_Y(y)}.\]








TipExample



Poisson.
Suppose \(X \sim \exp(\lambda)\) for some \(\lambda >0\), and given \(X=x\), \(Y\sim \text{Pois}(x)\). Find the conditional density of \(X|Y=y\) for some \(y\in \mathbb{Z}_+\).








TipExample



Suppose again \(X\) is a randomly chosen point between \(0\) and \(1\), and conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\) is a chosen as a random value between \(x\) and \(1\). (We can write this succinctly as \(Y|X=x \sim \text{Unif}[x,1]\)). Find the conditional pdf \(g(x | y)\) of \(X\) given \(Y=y\).
(Hint: Plug in \(y=0.1\) and \(y=0.9\) for a sanity check.)


Lastly, we will learn if \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent the conditional distribution (the pdf or pmf) of \(X|Y\) is the same as the marginal distribution (again, the pdf or pmf) of \(X\).






ImportantTheorem



\(X \perp Y\) \(\iff\) \(f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_{X}(x)\) for all \((x,y)\) with \(f_{Y}(y) >0\).

text:
Here is an interesting application of our tools (transforming random variables) from the previous section.
Take any random variable \(X\), and consider transforming it. When the transforming function is the cdf \(F_X(X)\), the result is a uniform number between 0 and 1. This is called the probability integral transformation.






ImportantLemma



Probability integral transformation.  Suppose \(X\) is a continuous random variable, \(Y=F_X(X)\), then \(Y\sim \text{Unif}[0,1]\).



Proof. Proof. (Hint: Start with the CDF of \(Y\). ) ◻

This helps us simulate a random number from any distribution. This is sometimes called the “inverse cdf method”.
Suppose \(Y\sim \text{Unif}[0,1]\). If \(F\) is a continuous cdf with quantile function \(F^{-1}\), then the random variable \(F^{-1}(Y)\) follows a distribution with cdf \(F\).
To simulate random numbers from \(F\):

First generate random numbers \(u_1, u_2,\cdots, u_n\) from \(\text{Unif}[0,1]\);
Then, apply inverse-cdf transform \(F^{-1}(u_i)\).

The resulting random numbers \(x_i = F^{-1}(u_i), i=1,\dots,n\) follow the distribution \(F\).






TipExample



Modeling Wait Times.
Suppose we want to simulate the time between arrivals at a coffee shop, modeled by an Exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda\) (which is used to model things like the time between radioactive decays or phone calls). The goal is to transform a “standard” random number \(U \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)\) – which every calculator can produce – into a wait time \(X\). How would one do this?


This is not just a theoretical exercise. Most computer software can only generate “pseudo-random” numbers from a \(\text{Unif}(0, 1)\) distribution. To get a random sample from an Exponential distribution, the computer also generates \(u\) from \(\text{Unif}(0,1)\) and simply calculates \(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln(u)\).

transformations of \(n\) random variables.

title: Lecture 14: More about moments
text:
When we are interested in the joint distribution of two random variables, it is useful to have a summary of how much the two random variables depend on each other. Covariance and correlation attempt to measure that dependence, (note, they only capture a particular type of dependence, namely linear dependence.)






NoteDefinition



Covariance.
For bivariate random variable \((X,Y)\), suppose \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu_X\) and \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu_Y\), \[\cov(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)],\] provided \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot]\) exists.


With the above definition, suppose the \(\sigma_X^2, \sigma_Y^2 <\infty\), then: \[\cov(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X] \mathbb{E}[Y].\]
For two random variables, covariance is a numerical summary of their relationship – about how do they vary together (linearly).






TipExample



Suppose the joint pdf of \((X,Y)\) is \[f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \left(2xy+\frac{1}{2}\right) \cdot 1_{x\in[0,1], y\in
      [0,1]}.\] Let us say we also know that \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[Y] = \frac{4}{3}\). (Make sure to try this on your own.)

Compute \(\mathbb{E}[XY] = \frac{25}{72}\).
Compute \(\cov(X,Y) = \frac{1}{144}\).



Here are some properties of covariance:

Covariance can be negative, while variance cannot be negative.
\(\cov(X,X)=V[X]\);
If \(X\perp Y\), \(\cov(X,Y) = 0\).
Even if \(\cov(X,Y) = 0\), \(X\) and \(Y\) can still be dependent.







TipExample



Zero covariance does not imply independence.
Take an random variable \(X\) that is equally likely to be -1, 0, or 11, as well as \(Y=X^2\). Calculate the covariance of \(X\) and \(Y\).


Zero covariance does imply independence.
Let us next examine the variance of linear sums of random variables. We can write that: \[V[X+Y] = V[X]+V[Y] +2 \cov(X,Y),\] More generally, \[V[aX+bY+c] =a^2 V[X]+ b^2V[Y] +2ab \times \cov(X,Y).\]






TipExample



What is \(V[X-Y]\)? What about when \(X \perp Y\)?








ImportantTheorem



Suppose \(V[X_i]<\infty\) for \(i=1,..,n\), \[V[ \sum \nolimits_{i=1}^n X_i] = \sum \nolimits_{i=1}^n  V[X_i]
  + 2 \sum \sum \nolimits_{i<j} \cov(X_i,X_j).\] If \(\{X_i\}_{i=1}^n\) are independent, \(V[ \sum \nolimits_{i=1}^n
X_i] = \sum \nolimits_{i=1}^n  V[X_i]\).


A key drawback of covariance is that it is not unit free. If you multiply \(X\) and \(Y\) by constants \(a\) and \(b\), we see that covariance grows by that amount: \[\cov(aX,bY) = ab \cov(X,Y).\]
So it is generally impossible to compare dependence across pairs of random variables based on covariances.
An easy fix is to rescale the covariance so that the new metric is comparable.






NoteDefinition



Correlation.
\[\corr(X,Y) = \frac{\cov(X,Y)}{
    \sqrt{V[X]} \sqrt{V[Y]}},\] Alternatively, \(\rho(X,Y) = \frac{\cov(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\)








ImportantTheorem



Size of correlation.
\(\rho(X,Y) \in [-1,1]\).








TipExample



Suppose \(X,Y\) have joint pdf \(f(x,y) = (x+y) \times 1(x\in [0,1],y\in [0,1])\).

Compute \(\cov(X,Y)\).
Compute \(\corr(X,Y)\).

text:
Conditional Expectations [DS 4.7] [Lec 14]
Recall expectation is a good one-number summary of a random variable. However, often you want a summary that takes into account additional information about another random phenomenon.
How to formally take the additional information into account? Conditional expectation is the tool of our choice.






NoteDefinition



Conditional Expectation (Mean).
Suppose we have random vector \((X,Y)\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[|Y|] < \infty\). A conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x]\) of \(Y\) given \(X=x\) is defined as follows:

If \(Y|X=x\) is continuous, \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x] = \int y f_{Y|X}(y|x)dy\)
If \(Y|X=x\) is discrete, \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x] = \sum y f_{Y|X}(y|x)\)



The conditioning information in the definition is \(X=x\), fixed as a specific value.
Generally, if you take \(X\) to be a random variable rather than a fixed value \(X=x\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X]\) is a random variable and a function of \(X\).
Intuitively, we should think of \(X=x\) as representing information that has been revealed to us. \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x]\) is our best guess of the value of \(Y\) given the information we have.
The “other” random variable \(X\) may or may not be related to \(Y\). In fact, it’s interesting to discuss the two extremes:

If \(X \perp Y\), the expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X] = \mathbb{E}[Y]\); it is unchanged even after observing \(X\).
If \(X=Y\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X] = X\); if we know \(X\), our best guess is \(X\) itself.

Note: Conditional expectation is also an expectation. Therefore, the properties of expectations – functions of random variables (Theorem [thm:lotus]), and linearity (Theorem [thm:linearity]) – also hold.






ImportantTheorem



Law of Iterated Expectation (LIE).
\[\mathbb{E} [\mathbb{E}[Y|X]] = \mathbb{E}[Y].\]



Proof. Proof. This is the “expectation” version of the Law of Total Probability \[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int yf_Y(y) dy = \int\int yf(x,y)dx dy
  = \int \left[\int yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy \right] f_{X}(x) dx\] whereas \(f_{Y}(y) =\int f(x,y)dx= \int  f_{Y|X}(y|x) f_{X}(x) dx.\) ◻

Suppose \(X\sim \text{Unif}(0,1)\), and \(Y|X=x \sim \text{Unif}(x,1)\). Compute \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) in the following two ways.

First compute the marginal probability density \(f_Y(y)\) of \(Y\). Then, use this to calculate the expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\).
Use the law of iterated expectation, i.e., \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y | X]]\).



Now, suppose we have a random variable \(Z = h(X,Y)\) that is a function of both random variables \(X\) and \(Y\). Then, \(\mathbb{E}[Z|X=x]\) can be calculated either as

Taking the conditional distribution of \(Z=h(X,Y)\), and calculating the conditional distribution of \(Z\) given \(X=x\), or
Taking the conditional distribution of \(r(x, Y)\) given \(X=x\).

This is formalized in the next lemma.






ImportantLemma



Conditioning is knowing.
Suppose \(Z=h(X,Y)\). Then, the conditional expectation of \(Z\) given \(X=x\) is: \[\mathbb{E}[Z|X=x] =\mathbb{E}[h(X,Y)|X=x]
    = \mathbb{E}[h({x},Y)|X=x].\] Further, if \(Z\) is continuous, \[\mathbb{E}[Z|X=x] = \int h(x,y)f_{Y|X}(y|x)dy\]








TipExample



Suppose \(X\sim f_X(x)\), and that \(Y=X^2\). Compute \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X]\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X|Y]\).


Knowing this, we can conveniently define an alternative form for a conditional expectation. First, define \(Z=h(X,Y)=Y\). Then, use the previous lemma to get: \[\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x] =\int y f_{Y|X}(y|x) dy.\] Then, use \(f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}\).






ImportantLemma



Alternative expression for conditional expectation.
Another formula for conditional expectation is: \[\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x] =

We are now used to the fact that \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x]\) is a best updated guess for \(Y\) after observing \(X=x\).
There is another important viewpoint to it. It turns out that, when you want to predict \(Y\) after having observed some value of \(X\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X]\) is a very good predictor of \(Y\).






ImportantTheorem



The conditional expectation predicts with the lowest mean squared error (MSE). Specifically, for the random vector \((X,Y)\), the prediction \(d(X)\) of \(Y\) such that its mean squared error \[\mathbb{E}[(Y-d(X))^2]\] is minimized with \(d(X)=\mathbb{E}[Y|X]\).


As we will see in our next lecture, the mean squared error of this optimal predictor \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X]\) is equal to the conditional variance. 2






TipExample



Let \(X\) be the number of patients out of the first 40 in a clinical trial who have been cured. Suppose that \(P\) has the uniform distribution on the interval [0,1] before the trial begins, and suppose that the outcomes of the patients are conditionally independent given \(P=p\).

What is a good prediction before the clinical trial starts?
What is the MSE-optimal prediction of \(P\) once you’ve observed \(X\)?



This is a simple but profound result. Given one random variable, our best guess (prediction) for another random variable is the conditional mean. We call this MSE-optimal prediction.

text:
Conditional Variance [DS 4.7] [Lec 14]
Recall we learned about the spread of a random variable \(X\) as the variance. Let us call this marginal variance. We will extend this notion to the variability conditional on another random variable \(X\).






NoteDefinition



For the random vector \((X,Y)\), \[V[Y|X=x] =\mathbb{E}[ (Y- \mathbb{E}[Y|X=x])^2|X=x] .\]


As \(X\) is a random variable, \(V[Y|X]\) is also a random variable and a function of \(X\).






TipExample



Take joint pdf \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = (x+y) \times 1((x,y)\in [0,1]^2)\) of a random vector \((X,Y)\). The conditional expectation of \(Y\) given \(X=x\) is \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X] = \frac{\frac{1}{2} X + \frac{1}{3}}{X + \frac{1}{2}}\) for \(0 \le X \le 1\). What is \(V[Y|X]\)?


Next, we learn about a key relationship between marginal variance and conditional variance.






ImportantTheorem



Law of total variance.
Also known as Eve’s law: \[V[Y] = E[V[Y|X]] +V[E[Y|X]].\]


Often when the value of the random variable \(X=x\) is revealed, there is less uncertainty about the other random variable \(Y\). That is, the conditional variance \(V[Y|X=x]\) of \(Y\) is smaller than the marginal variance \(V[Y]\).
Here is an example of this.






TipExample



Let us revisit the example of a two-step model where (1) \(X\) is uniform between 0 and 1, and (2) given \(X=x\), \(Y\) is uniform between \(x\) and \(1\).

Calculate \(V[Y|X=x]\).
Calculate \(V[Y]\)
Compare the size of the two (in a graph over values \(0 \le X \le 1\)).



But the reduction in variance is not guaranteed. Take random variable \(Z=XY\) for independent random variables \(X \perp Y\), where \(X\) is equally likely to be \(0\) or \(1\), and \(Y\) is Normal with mean zero and variance 1. Then, the marginal variance is:
\[V[Z] = 1/2.\]
and the conditional variance is
\[V[Z|X=x] = V[xY] = x^2 V[Y] = x^2.\]
Clearly, if \(x\) is bigger than \(\sqrt{1/2}\), the conditional variance \(V[Z|X=x]\) is larger than \(X\). Put another way, there is positive probability that the variance actually increases:
\[\mathbb{P}\left( V[Z|X] > V[Z] \right) = \mathbb{P}\left( X^2 > \frac{1}{2} \right) \simeq 0.707 > 0.\]
So, in what sense is the variance reduced when \(X\) is revealed? On average (in plain language), or in expectation:






ImportantTheorem



Conditional Variance vs. Marginal Variance.
\[V[Y] \ge E[V[Y|X]].\]


The proof is simple: examine the law of total variance.

Convergence in probability.

section: The Law of Large Numbers [DS 6.2-6.3, AOS 6.1-6.3] [Lec 16]
text:
The Law of Large Numbers [DS 6.2-6.3, AOS 6.1-6.3] [Lec 16]
In various applications, the sample mean, or sample average: \[\bar X_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n X_i = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n}{n}\] is of key importance. We will use \(\bar X\) to denote the average of \(n\) random variables \(X_1,\cdots, X_n\).
What would happen as \(n\to \infty\)? In particular, does \(\bar X_n\) converge as \(n\to \infty\)? If so, (1) in what sense and (2) to what value does \(\bar X_n\) converge to?
We can be more concrete. Let’s say we throw a coin multiple times, and record the numbers as \(X_1, \cdots, X_n\). We can inuit (expect) that the average \((X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n)/n\) will be close to \(0.5\).
The laws of large numbers establishes this rigorously, in a fairly general setting.

Basic properties of sample mean
Before answering the question of \(n\to \infty\), we first examine properties of the sample mean when \(n\) is finite.

The mean of sample mean is \[\mathbb{E}[\bar X_n] = \mathbb{E}[X_1],\] (provided that \(\mathbb{E}[X_1]\) exists).
The variance of sample mean is \[V(\bar X_n)= \frac{1}{n}V(X_1),\] (provided that \(V(X_1)\) exists.)

Next, we learn our first, celebrated result about how the sample mean probabilistically converges to the true mean.






ImportantTheorem



Weak Law of Large Numbers.
For iid sample \(X_1,...,X_n\) whose mean and variance exist, \[\bar X_n \;\ipto \;\mathbb{E}[X_1].\]


The qualifier “weak” is for convergence in probability – wLLN for short. (There is also a strong law of large numbers, which is beyond the scope of this class.)

Proof. Proof. Recall Chebyshev inequality. For random variable \(X\) (whose variance exists), we have \[\mathbb{P}(|X-\mathbb{E}[X] |>t ) \le V(X)/t^2.\]
Next, for iid \(X_i\)’s, \[\mathbb{P}( |\bar X_n- \mathbb{E}[X_1] | \ge t) \le \frac{V(X_1)}{nt^2}.\]
As \(t>0\) is arbitrary1, we can choose it to be very small. This proves that: \[\bar X_n \ipto \mathbb{E}[X_1].\] ◻





image



Next, we examine an interesting application of wLLN.






TipExample



Histogram.
A histogram is the result of binning data \(X_1,\cdots, X_n\) and measuring the relative frequency in the bins. The histogram height from a bin between \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) is \[\bar Y_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n1(X_i\in [c_1,c_2)
    )\] for some interval \([c_1,c_2)\). \(\bar Y_n\) is the sample mean of iid Bernoulli random variables.
By wLLN, \[\bar Y_n \ipto \mathbb{E}[1(X_1\in [c_1,c_2)] = \mathbb{P}(X_i \in [c_1,c_2)).\]








TipExample



Determine the required sample size.
Suppose \(X_1,...,X_n\distras{iid} F\) whose mean and variance exist, and we have an upper bound on \(V(X_1)\), say \(V_0\), we have \[\mathbb{P}( |\bar X_n- \mathbb{E}[X_1] | \ge t) \le \frac{V_0}{nt^2}.\] In other words, with probability at least \(1- \frac{V_0}{nt^2}\), \[|\bar X_n- \mathbb{E}[X_1] | \le t.\]
Suppose we have a target/tolerable error \(t_0\). We can choose the sample size \(n\) to control the probability bound \[1- \frac{V_0}{nt_0^2}.\]
For instance, \(t_0=0.01\), \(V_0=1\), if we hope to achieve 99% confidence, what sample size \(n\) is needed?


Note, we have required that the variance is finite (\(V[X_i]<\infty\)).
Strong Law of large numbers.

title: Lec 16: Convergence of Random variables
text:
The Central Limit Theorem [DS 6.2-6.3, AOS 6.1-6.3] [Lec 16]
We finally arrive at the central limit theorem (CLT) which provides a simple yet powerful way of approximating probabilities.






ImportantTheorem



Central Limit Theorem.
Take \(X_1,X_2,...,X_n\) that are independent random variables each with mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_1] =\mu\) and \(V[X_1] =\sigma^2\). Then for each fixed number \(t\), \[\lim_{n\to \infty} \mathbb{P}( \sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n -\mu)/\sigma \le t ) = \Phi(t),\] where \(\Phi(t)\) is the cdf of a standard normal (\(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)) random variable. We write this as \[\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n -\mu)/\sigma  \idto N(0,1).\]



Proof. Proof. The mgf of \(\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n -\mu)/\sigma\) with \(X_i\)’s mgf \(\psi\): \[\psi_n(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{t \sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n -\mu)/\sigma}]
= \mathbb{E}[e^ {\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n
  (\frac{X_i-\mu}{\sigma})}   ].\] We would like to use Theorem [thm:mgf-converge]; so, the goal is to show \(\psi_n(t) \to e^{t^2/2}\) for \(t\) in some interval around \(t=0\).
Let \(Y_i =\frac{X_i-\mu}{\sigma}\), so \(Y_i, i=1\cdots,n\) are iid with mean \(0\) and variance \(1\). With the Taylor expansion: \[\psi_Y(t) = \psi_Y(0) + \psi_Y^{(1)}(0) t + \frac{1}{2!} \psi_Y^{(2)}(0) t^2
+ \frac{1}{3!} \psi_Y^{(3)}(0) t^3+...,\] it follows that \[\psi_n(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^ {\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i    }   ] = [\psi_Y({t}/{\sqrt{n}})]^n
\to e^{t^2/2}.\] ◻

A direct implication is that: for \(n\) large enough, \[\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n -\mu)/\sigma   \approx N(0,1).\] which means that the “standardized” random variable \(\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n -\mu)/\sigma\) with a large but fixed \(n\) follows the standard Normal distribution.
Since we know very well how to handle Normal random variables and how to calculate probabilities from them, the CLT provides a simple yet powerful way of approximating probabilities.






TipExample



Normal approximation.
In many cases, for \(n\) being a few tens, the approximation is reasonably accurate.

Suppose \(X_i \distras{iid} Ber(p)\) for \(i=1,..,n\), and \(n=100\). We can apply the Normal approximation to the following probability \[\mathbb{P}(\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^n X_i \ge 70).\]
Suppose \(X_i \distras{iid} Pois(\lambda)\) for \(i=1,..,n\), and \(n=100\). We can apply the Normal approximation to the following probability \[\mathbb{P}( |\bar{X}_n-\lambda|<c).\]
Suppose \(X_i \distras{iid} Exp(\lambda)\) for \(i=1,..,n\), and \(n=100\). We can apply the Normal approximation to the following probability \[\mathbb{P}( |\bar{X}_n- \lambda|<c).\]

Let \(X_1, \dots , X_{125}\) be the number of errors in the programs. What is the probability of the average number of errors being not so high, say within 0.5 of the mean 5?

Suppose \(X_i \distras{iid} Pois(\lambda)\) for \(i=1,..,n\). Determine \(n\) such that \[\mathbb{P}( |\bar{X}_n-\lambda|< 0.1 ) > 0.95.\] Alternatively, the Chebyshev inequality can also be used to provide an answer. Which one is more accurate?
